Regarding This Volume

Volume 5 is a record of uprisings, protests, regime overthrows, civil wars, and coups in 49 countries south of the Sahara. The regional composition and country order follow the Country Analysis Series (2026-10-07). The method of description, dataset definitions, rules for connecting countries, and axioms and formulas are described in Volume 1.

The numbers in the table below represent the number of records linked to this country in each dataset, as counted by the program from the raw data. A value of 0 indicates that there are no records in the corresponding dataset, and the magnitude of the numbers varies according to the definitions, thresholds, and reporting scope of the datasets (Volume 1, Part 4).

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The Herero and Nama Uprisings of 1904–1908 and German Troops' Massacres Uprising · 1904–1908

According to SAHO chronology, German authorities confiscated the land and large herds of livestock of the Herero in 1888, and German troops were suppressing the southern Bondelswarts uprising in 1903. According to the Mémorial de la Shoah, the uprising began on January 12, 1904, when Okahandja Herero attacked German farms and shops, and General Lothar von Trotha issued an extermination order on October 2 after the attack on Waterberg on August 11. In 1905, the Nama entered guerrilla resistance and Hendrik Witbooi was killed (SAHO), and in 1907 the Nama resistance ended with the death of Jacobus Marengo. The war was officially ended on March 31, 1907, and the concentration camps were closed on January 27, 1908. The memorial materials note that mortality at Shark Island Concentration Camp off Lüderitz was particularly high. On May 28, 2021, German Foreign Minister Heiko Maas officially designated the event as a 'genocide from today's perspective' and announced an 11-billion-euro support package over 30 years, but characterized it as a sign of recognition rather than legal reparation. A Namibian government spokesperson described it as 'the first step in the right direction,' while Paramount Chief Vekuii Rukoro of the Herero criticized it as Namibia's 'complete surrender.' The German government describes it in terms of political and moral responsibility, while some representatives of the Herero and Nama describe it in terms of reparations.

Deaths (Nama)UnconfirmedApprox. 10,000 (50% of the population; Shoah Memorial; Al Jazeera 2021 reports the same)

The Nama resistance (1905–1907) and concentration camp deaths (~1908) fall outside this period. In the COW civil war data, this war does not appear in the Namibia entry (colonial era).

The 1922 Bondelswarts Uprising and Aerial Bombing Uprising · 1922

According to the SAHO chronology, the South African federal administration clashed with the southern Nama group of Bondelswarts over cattle taxes and arrests in 1921, and after the 'Maurice incident' in May 1922, troops were sent to suppress them, killing some women and children. Rodney Warwick (LitNet, 2022) states that the uprising took place from late May to early June 1922; a detachment of two DH.9 biplanes commanded by Major Pierre van Rynvelt bombed Grootfontein, and on June 2, aircraft bombed and machine-gunned the Koonuanib Gorge. On June 3, Maurice, a Bondelswarts leader, was mortally wounded in an ambush at Bergkamper and died the next day. 14,000 livestock were confiscated. The League of Nations Mandates Commission summoned the administrator, Hofmeyr, criticizing the pre-consultation approach and the dual role of the administrator as military commander. The federal government described it as the suppression of armed resistance to tax and law enforcement, while the Bondelswarts side and subsequent scholarship describe it as an uprising by a community that had lost its means of livelihood.

Government Troop CasualtiesUnconfirmed2 killed (1 at Drifhok, 1 in a second ambush), 7 wounded at Bergkamper (Warwick)

Shooting at Old Location, Windhoek on December 10, 1959 Protest · 1959

According to Henning Melber (The Conversation, 2023), in late 1959 residents of Windhoek's Old Location protested against forced relocation to Katutura by means of a women-led boycott of municipal services. On December 10, when stones were thrown at a meeting with white officials, police opened fire, killing 13 unarmed protesters and injuring more than 40. Among the dead was one woman, Anna Mungunda, who became an icon of resistance. From 1960, residents were relocated to Katutura and Commusdal, and the location was officially closed in 1968. The SAHO chronology describes this as a 'riot' against the expansion of urban apartheid, noting that the UN General Assembly passed a resolution criticizing South African rule in the same year, November. Melber describes the founding of SWAPO in 1960 as a response to this event. Namibia observes December 10 as a public holiday for Human Rights Day (also Women's Day). The authorities at the time described it as restoring order, while residents and liberation movements describe it as a massacre.

The 1966–1989 War of Independence and the 1989 UN-Supervised Elections Civil War · 1966–1990

According to the SAHO chronology, in 1960 Toivo ya Toivo and Sam Nujoma reorganized the OPO as SWAPO and began guerrilla training, and in 1966 the first military action of SWAPO took place in Owamboland. Namibia commemorates August 26 (Omwahulugwembe) as Heroes' Day. In 1968 Toivo ya Toivo was sentenced to 20 years in prison at a Pretoria terrorism trial, and in 1971 the International Court of Justice ruled South Africa's presence illegal. Up to 20,000 South African troops were stationed in Namibia by 1983 (SAHO). Following the New York Accords of December 1988, the UN Transition Assistance Group (UNTAG) implemented the independence plan from April 1, 1989. According to UN records, voter turnout in the Constituent Assembly election of November 7–11, 1989 was 97%, with SWAPO winning 41 seats, the Democratic Turnhalle Alliance 21 seats, and minor parties 10 seats, and Namibia became independent on March 21, 1990. The South African government describes it as a counterinsurgency operation; SWAPO and the UN describe it as a struggle for national liberation.

General Strike of Contract Workers, 1971–1972 Protest · 1971–1972

According to Heike Becker (The Namibian, 2026), the December 1971 strike began almost spontaneously at a fish-processing plant in Walvis Bay where 3,200 contract workers were employed, and on Monday, December 13, Owamboland workers in Windhoek refused to work and stayed in their lodgings. Nationwide, 16,000 contract workers went on strike. The demands included the abolition of the contract labor system, freedom to choose workplace and occupation, wage increases, permission to bring families, and the abolition of movement controls. Two days later, the authorities returned the striking workers to Owamboland, where a strike committee was formed and a rally of 3,500 people was held on January 10, 1972. The authorities offered the abolition of the recruitment agency Swanla and its replacement by the Department of Tribal Labour while strongly restricting political expression and mobilization; by May 1972, 267 people had been detained under emergency regulations in Owamboland. Prosecutions of 'ringleaders' eventually collapsed. Authorities described it as a labor dispute and a security issue; workers and liberation movement sides described it as resistance against the contract labor system.

1999 Caprivi Separatist Armed Attacks and Treason Trial Uprising · 1999–2015

According to Amnesty International (2003), on August 2, 1999, the separatist group Caprivi Liberation Army (CLA) armed attacked government forces and public offices in the Caprivi region of northeastern Namibia; the government declared a state of emergency and detained more than 300 people on suspicion of participating in, sympathizing with, or supporting the attack. 122 were detained while facing charges of high treason, murder, and other offenses. Amnesty stated that many defendants suffered torture and harsh treatment and poor detention conditions, and some appeared to have been arrested solely for nonviolent support of the opposition or ethnic identity; it also noted that 12 defendants had died in police custody by October 2003. The Namibian Sun (2014) reported that police stations, military bases, border posts, and a broadcasting station in Katima Mulilo were targets of the attack, in which 8 people died. The same report stated that initially 132 people had been charged with 278 counts, that 43 were released in February 2013, and that more than 20 had died in custody. The government describes the response as law enforcement against an armed rebellion, while defendants and human rights organizations describe prolonged detention and torture.

2. Pre-Industrial Revolution (~1759) — Records of Uprisings and Civil War

First Khoikhoi–Dutch War Early Dutch East India Company (VOC) settlement at the Cape · 1659–1660

According to South African History Online (SAHO), conflict began when the Khoikhoi leader Doman and his followers seized seven oxen used by the company as draft animals after VOC settlements encroached on grazing land. Doman was wounded in the Battle of 19 July 1659 and withdrew to Saldanha Bay. The war ended around April–May 1660 when the Dutch made peace with the Gorinhaikwa and Goringhaiqua, after which the Khoikhoi lost more land to settlers. Doman died in December 1663, and by 1676 the Khoikhoi had been excluded from settlement near the fort. VOC records describe it as a response to livestock theft; from the Khoikhoi perspective, it was resistance against loss of grazing land.

  1. South African History Online — The establishment of the Cape and its impact on the Khoikhoi and Dutch · Public history DB · Orientation: South African nonprofit history DB, anti-apartheid and subjugated-group perspective — https://www.sahistory.org.za/article/establishment-cape-and-its-impact-khoikhoi-and-dutch

Second Khoikhoi–Dutch War (Kochoqua Campaign) VOC expansion at the Cape · 1673–

According to SAHO, the start of the Second War was the VOC Policy Council's dispatch of a punitive expedition to Kochoqua in 1673. Defeated repeatedly, the Khoikhoi lost their independence and many were forced into servile labor; after the war, the VOC seized land on the basis of conquest and distributed it to farmers. The SAHO page linked in this round contains no year of cessation (traditionally known as 1677), no name of a Kochoqua leader, and no number of livestock seized.

  1. South African History Online — The establishment of the Cape and its impact on the Khoikhoi and Dutch · Public history DB · Orientation: South African nonprofit history DB, anti-apartheid and subjugated-group perspective — https://www.sahistory.org.za/article/establishment-cape-and-its-impact-khoikhoi-and-dutch

3. 1760–1815 — Literature

The 1808 Slave Uprising in Mauritius 1808

According to SAHO, the uprising began on the evening of 27 October 1808 when nine men, including the enslaved carpenter Louis (in his early twenties), the Irishmen James Hooper and Michael Kelly, and several enslaved and Khoikhoi men, plotted a rebellion. They marched through rural areas, gathering slaves and servants to enter Cape Town and seize the Amsterdam Battery; more than 300 slaves and servants joined them along the way, and 340 raided some 30 grain farms. The uprising was suppressed about 36 hours after it began when it encountered infantry and cavalry at Salt River, and 326 people were captured. Forty-seven went to trial; Louis and Hooper were sentenced to death for treason, eleven to death for 'active participation', and the rest received commutations, including imprisonment on Robben Island. SAHO notes that news of the Haitian Revolution (1791–1804) influenced the uprising's planning. The colonial authorities described it as a rebellion; subsequent historical accounts describe it as the first large-scale anti-slavery movement in Cape Colony.

  1. South African History Online — Louis van Mauritius and the slave revolt of 1808 · Public history DB · Orientation: South African nonprofit history DB, anti-apartheid and subjugated-group perspective — https://sahistory.org.za/article/louis-van-mauritius-and-slave-revolt-1808

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

1906 Bambatha (Nkabatha) Uprising Uprising · 1906

According to SAHO, in 1906 in the Natal Colony, growing Zulu anger over the poll tax led to an uprising led by Chief Bambatha. This uprising is described as the last armed resistance against white rule before the establishment of the Union of South Africa. SAHO states that 4,000 Zulus and 30 whites died; some Zulus fought on the side of the Natal government and were killed. The colonial government spent £740,000, with over 7,000 imprisoned and 4,000 flogged. Chiefs who supported the rebellion were sentenced to death for treason but had their sentences commuted to life exile on St. Helena. Dinuzulu was captured near Nongoma, tried in Greytown, sentenced to four years' imprisonment for treason, and deported to Rustenburg in Transvaal. In 1910, the chiefs were pardoned. The colonial government described it as resistance to tax refusal and suppression of the rebellion, while Zulu accounts and subsequent scholarship describe it as resistance against taxation and land pressure.

Sharpeville Massacre and Langa Shootings on March 21, 1960 Protest · 1960

According to SAHO, on March 21, 1960, the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), led by Robert Sobukwe, appealed to its supporters to leave their passes at home and go to the police station to volunteer for arrest. Police opened fire on a crowd gathered in front of the Sharpeville police station, killing 69 people; the official inquest reported 180 seriously wounded. Drum journalist Tyler wrote that more than 200 Africans were shot. In Langa, Cape Town, three people died and 26 were injured on the same day. In Pretoria, Durban, and East London, police recorded only the names of protesters without making arrests. SAHO notes that the ANC and PAC were banned in the subsequent 1960s. The government at the time described it as police responding to a threat, while the PAC and victims' side describe it as a massacre of an unarmed crowd.

Soweto Student Uprising of June 16, 1976 Uprising · 1976–1977

According to SAHO, the immediate trigger was the 'Afrikaans Medium Instruction' order that made Afrikaans a language of instruction on par with English. The dates within the SAHO article itself differ (1974 vs. 1975). Students regarded Afrikaans as 'the oppressor's language.' On June 16, 1976, a student march took place in Soweto, with an estimated 1,000 to 10,000 participants. By the third day, it had spread to townships around Soweto and other areas, spreading to schools in Kaggies, Tembisa, Alexandra, East and West Rand, and Cape Town, continuing into the following year. The government officially announced 23 deaths, but other reports estimated at least 200, and the Silie Commission appointed by the government reported 575 deaths. The government describes it as a suppression of unrest, while the student and liberation movement sides describe it as an uprising against apartheid education.

July 2021 KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng Unrest Protest · 2021

According to the government news agency SAnews (2022-04-01), President Ramaphosa stated in his opening remarks at the July unrest national inquiry hearing by the South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) that at least 350 people died and at least 50 billion rand were lost from the economy, with at least 2 million jobs lost or affected over 'one week and one day' of unrest in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng in July 2021. He viewed the unrest as partly driven by individuals deliberately inciting destruction while social and economic conditions also played a role. The page for this round contains no account of the trigger for the unrest (the imprisonment of former President Zuma). The government describes it as incitement to economic destruction, whereas other accounts cite socioeconomic factors such as poverty and unemployment alongside it.

5. Modern Events through the Lens of Literature

First Gun War (Ntoa ya Lithunya) — 1880–1881 — Uprising against the Cape colonial government's disarmament Uprising · 1880–1881

According to the SAHO Lesotho entry, on March 12, 1868, Governor Wodehouse proclaimed Basutoland a British protectorate, and it was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1871. The Dictionary of South African English (DSAE) entry on the Gun War defines this war as the 1880–81 conflict that arose from the Cape government's attempt to disarm the Basotho, stating that fighting began when the Basotho refused to surrender their firearms in 1880 and continued from September 1880 to April 1881. Citing Vigne (1972), the same entry notes that the war cost the colony approximately £3 million, ended with the collapse of Cape authority in Basutoland, and led to the Cape's return of the territory to imperial authorities in 1884. Mailer (1986) describes this as a rare successful African resistance against colonial rule in southern Africa, while the Cape government's account and subsequent accounts of the Basotho victory describe it as resistance to preserve land and sovereignty.

Invalidation of the 1970 Election and the BCP Uprising in January 1974 Regime Overthrow · 1970–1974

According to an article by Joseph Ngwawi of the Southern African Research and Documentation Centre (SARDC) under SADC, after independence in October 1966, when the Basotho Congress Party (BCP) led by Ntsu Mokhehle won the 1970 election, Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan declared a state of emergency, invalidated the election, suspended the constitution, and banned political parties. King Moshoeshoe II was placed under house arrest and went into exile for eight months. In January 1974, Mokhehle attempted a coup but was suppressed, and many of his supporters were imprisoned. The SAHO Lesotho entry notes that only in 1993 did 23 years of authoritarian rule (including seven years of military rule) end and constitutional governance be restored. The Jonathan government described these measures as actions to maintain order, while the BCP side described them as an extension of rule by seizing election results.

Casualties and Detentions in the 1974 UprisingUnconfirmedMany supporters imprisoned (SARDC, no figures)

Archigos records Jonathan's tenure as a single period from 1966-10-04 to 1986-01-20, recording no break in 1970.

Military Coups in 1986 and 1991 and the King's Suspension of Parliament in 1994 Coups · 1986–1994

According to the SARDC article, in January 1986, a quasi-military force led by Lieutenant General Justin Lekhanya overthrew the Jonathan government, and in April 30, 1991, a coup led by Lieutenant General Elias Ramaema forced Lekhanya to step down as chairman of the military council. In the first multiparty election in 23 years in 1993, the BCP won overwhelmingly, but the Basotho National Party (BNP) contested the results. Clashes between military units occurred in January 1994, Deputy Prime Minister Sello Molapo was assassinated in mid-April, and at least four people died in unrest during the king's suspension of parliament on August 17. The Mokhehle government was restored on September 14. A briefing by the South African Parliament Joint Committee (1998) notes that SADC's request to South Africa, Botswana, and Mozambique for a mission to Lesotho following the 1994 coup was its first intervention. The military and royal sides described it as restoring order in the political crisis, while the elected government side described it as an interruption of constitutional governance.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
Deaths in August 1994 unrestUnconfirmedAt least 4 (SARDC)

Data record: Powell & Thyne record all three events of 1986-01-20, 1991-04-30, and 1994-08-17 as successful coups; Archigos records Jonathan and Lekhanya's departures as 'military irregular exits' and Mokhehle's 1994 departure as an 'irregular exit by other government actors', and records Letsie III's tenure of 1994-08-17 to 09-14 as an irregular entry. The internal military clashes in January 1994 and the assassination of a deputy prime minister in April are not recorded in UCDP.

1998 election dispute, military mutiny, and SADC military intervention (Operation Boreas) Civil War · 1998

According to the SARDC article, when the Lesotho Congress for Democracy (LCD) won 79 of 80 seats in the May 23, 1998 election, the opposition alleged fraud; on September 11, junior officers arrested 29 senior officers. The South African Parliament joint committee briefing (1998-11-02) states that the Rangas Commission found some irregularities but could not prove government responsibility, and that mutineers removed military command structures while streets descended into anarchy. At the request of the Lesotho Prime Minister, South Africa and Botswana launched Operation Boreas on September 22, 1998. Mail & Guardian (1998-09-25) reported that approximately 600 South African soldiers faced at least 2,000 LDF troops supported by armed civilians, and that residents responding to opposition appeals burned and looted most of Maseru's central commercial district. On October 2, all parties agreed on a transitional structure (PMG), and a timetable for the 2000 rerun election was set (SARDC). The South African government and SADC characterized it as a regional peace intervention at the request of the legitimate government; LDF soldiers and some opposition factions described it as a foreign invasion (Mail & Guardian).

Data record: UCDP/PRIO records government-versus-military factional conflict (conflict_id 411) as an 'internationalized internal conflict' for the year 1998 alone (under war criteria, fewer than 1,000 deaths). Powell & Thyne do not record the 1998 mutiny as a coup. NAVCO 1.3 records the 1997–2002 'fair election campaign' as nonviolent and partially successful. ACLED tallies 9 protests, 24 political violence events, and 96 fatalities in 1998.

August 30, 2014 military attack on police (controversy over coup attempt) and the death of Mahao in 2015 Coup · 2014–2016

According to the SARDC article, in June 2014 Prime Minister Thomas Thabane suspended parliament ahead of a no-confidence vote, and on August 30 a coup plot was alleged but denied by the military. IOL (2014-09-29) reported that on the morning of August 30 soldiers moved to the homes of the prime minister, one minister, and the military commander as well as the headquarters of the Lesotho Mounted Police Service, killing one policeman and injuring nine; Thabane had reportedly fled just before receiving a tip-off. At a meeting in Pretoria on September 1, it was decided to dispatch SADC mediators (SARDC). According to the South African Institute for Security Studies (ISS, 2016-01-20), Major General Maaparankoe Mahao was appointed as successor to Commander Thulare Kamoli, who had been dismissed; after early elections in February 2015 brought the Motsoahae-led coalition to power, Kamoli returned. In June 2015 soldiers loyal to Kamoli went to arrest Mahao on suspicion of involvement in a mutiny plot and killed him. SADC established an investigative commission chaired by Judge Pius Langa of Botswana; when the government refused to accept the report, SADC demanded its publication and implementation at the January 2016 summit. The 2017/18 Amnesty International report states that the SADC commission concluded that Mahao had been murdered deliberately, and that eight LDF members appeared in court on December 1, 2017, charged with involvement in his killing. The military denied a coup plot (SARDC), while Thabane's side describes it as an attempted coup. Mahao's death is described by the Motsoahae government as having been killed during arrest resistance and by Thabane's side as a cold-blooded murder (ISS).

Archigos 4.1 lacks an entry for the post-2015 period and therefore does not capture the change in leadership at this time. ACLED records 3 political violence events and 1 death in 2014, and 5 political violence events and 4 deaths in 2015.

September 5, 2017 assassination of Defense Force Commander Mochochoka Coup · 2017

According to the Amnesty International 2017/18 report, on March 1, 2017, parliament passed a motion of no confidence against Prime Minister Motsoahae and on March 7 the king dissolved parliament; following elections on June 3, Thabane's All Basotho Convention (ABC)-led coalition took power. On June 14, the day before his inauguration, Thabane's estranged wife, Lepelle Thabane, was killed. On September 5, Commander Quntaletso Mochochoka of the Lesotho Defense Force was shot and killed in his office at the LDF headquarters in Maseru; the suspects, Lieutenant General Butholezile Sechele and Colonel Tepo Hachache of the LDF, were also killed by return fire. The prime minister announced an investigation, but no progress information was available by year-end. In August of the same year, SADC extended the term of a committee overseeing implementation of recommendations made by the commission established in 2015 following the political unrest. Of the 23 LDF officers charged with mutiny, the remaining 22 were acquitted on all charges by a military court on December 18.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

November 1994 Murder of Segametsi Mogomotsi and Student Unrest in Mochudi and Gaborone Protest · 1994

According to Mmegi (2015-04-27), on November 6, 1994, the mutilated body of 14-year-old female student Segametsi Mogomotsi was found near her family's home in Mochudi. This death sparked unrest in Mochudi that spread to other areas including Gaborone, with violent protests occurring at several schools, universities, and the University of Botswana. The investigation involved Scottish investigators who interviewed the family; however, as of the article date (2015), the police had not reported progress for years, and the family expressed disappointment with the government. In 2012, a regional council chair requested a meeting with the presidency on behalf of the family but stated that there was no response. The government describes this as an ongoing criminal investigation being pursued by the police; the family and residents describe it as an unexplained case.

Central Kalahari Game Reserve Bushman Relocation and Litigation, 1997–2006 Protest · 1997–2006

According to Mail & Guardian (2006-12-13), the Botswana government relocated approximately 2,000 San (Basarwa) from the Central Kalahari Game Reserve (the size of Belgium) primarily in 1997 and 2002, stating that all but about 24 left voluntarily. On December 13, 2006, the High Court ruled 2–1 in favor of the San, finding that more than 1,000 San were unjustly evicted from their ancestral hunting grounds and could return. Judge Paniafi, who delivered the judgment, said cutting off food rations and hunting permits together was tantamount to starving out remaining residents, while Judge Unity Dow found that the 2002 relocation was forced and illegal without consent. Chief Justice Dikgang Moseneke dissented in an opinion rejecting the lawsuit. The government argued that the San posed a threat to wildlife and that the reserve was a poverty trap blocking access to health and education; the court found no basis for the San's claim that the government and De Beers sought to clear the land for diamond mining. Roy Sesana, a representative of a San pressure group, welcomed the ruling. The government characterized it as a policy for welfare and conservation; the San side described it as forced eviction.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
Number RelocatedApproximately 2,000, plus voluntary relocation of about 24 (Botswana government, cited by Mail & Guardian)More than 1,000 unjustly evicted (High Court majority opinion, 2006-12-13) / More than 1,000 hoping to return (activists)

Data Record: Because this was legal and civil society resistance rather than violent conflict, it appears in none of UCDP, COW, or NAVCO. Whether MM or ACLED's protest counts for the relevant years include this case could not be verified. The category is classified as nonviolent resistance and placed under 'Protest.'

Public Sector General Strike and Dismissals of Essential Workers, April–June 2011 Protest · 2011

According to the Botswana Government Daily News (2026-03-12), Minister Moeti Mokomele stated in parliament that the 2011 public sector dispute met the legal requirements for a lawful strike, but the participation of essential workers who could threaten public life, safety, and health was illegal. In this process, 2,802 people were dismissed; of these, 2,700 applied for reinstatement, and 1,834 were reinstated in November 2011, with an additional 245 reinstated under a 2019 decision. They were rehired on two-year contracts rather than reinstated, and the government stated that all dismissed workers received retirement benefits. According to the U.S. Department of State's 2012 Human Rights Report, union sources claimed filing 15 lawsuits related to the strike, with BOFEPUSU winning or settling favorably in 13 cases. As of year-end, two cases involving the deregistration of BOFEPUSU and dismissals of 'essential' workers were pending, and the government added teachers, veterinarians, and diamond workers to the list of essential services in response to the strike. The government describes this as dismissals for violating essential service provisions; the union side characterizes it as a violation of the right to strike.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

King's Proclamation of April 12, 1973 — Abolition of the 1968 Constitution and Ban on Political Parties Regime Overthrow · 1973

According to the SAHO entry, Swaziland gained full independence on September 6, 1968; in 1973 King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution, and in 1977 a new constitution made the king an absolute ruler. Musa Hlophe, mediator of the Swazi Civil Society Coalition (SCCCO), writing in the Mail & Guardian (2005-04-18), states that the April 12 proclamation outlawed political parties, placed legislative, executive, and judicial power under the king, and abolished a bill of rights, from which a de facto state of emergency began and had reached its 32nd year by April 12, 2005. The same article describes the 2004 constitutional draft as also barring parties from participating in elections. The royal family and government describe this proclamation as a return to traditional governance, while the opposition and civil society describe it as a suspension of constitutional rule.

Deposition of Regent Dzeliwe in 1983 — 'Quiet Palace Coup' Coup · 1982–1983

According to the Christian Science Monitor (1983-08-24), a power vacuum emerged when Sobhuza II, who had reigned for 61 years, died on August 6, 1982. In early 1983, the 'moderate reformers' known as the Mabandla (Mbandla) Dlamini prime minister stepped down, and Prince Bhekimpi became prime minister; new cabinet members and others deposed Regent Dzeliwe, the late king's senior wife. Princess Ntombi, the young queen and mother of the heir, became the new regent. The article describes this as a 'quiet palace coup' without reports of arrests or unrest, framing the conflict as traditionalists versus modernizers while noting that it was also a clash between personalities. The article states that the 1978 constitution banned opposition parties. The SAHO entry notes that Makhosetive Dlamini was chosen as successor in 1982 and ascended the throne as Mswati III in 1986.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Casualties / DetentionsUnconfirmedNo reports of arrests or unrest (CSM 1983-08-24)

Data Record: Powell & Thyne records the event on 1983-08-10 as a successful coup, while Archigos records Dzeliwe's tenure as 1982-08-21 to 1983-08-10 and classifies her departure as 'an irregular transfer of power by other government actors without foreign support.' Deposition dates diverge (August 9 [several encyclopedic sources], August 10 [P&T · Archigos], October house arrest [some sources]), and the annual page (CSM) does not specify an exact date.

1995 Riots and 1990s Labor Union Strikes Protest · 1995–1998

According to the SAHO entry, the first parliamentary elections were held in 1993, and in the 1995 riots, the parliament building and the homes of the prime minister and deputy vice-chancellor of the University of Swaziland were burned. In late 1997, the king's powers were somewhat reduced, but after the 1998 elections, the king retained most power, opposition parties remained banned, labor unions organized strikes and import boycotts, and the Public Order Act was passed. The government emphasized maintaining public order, while the unions and opposition demanded political reform.

  1. South African History Online — Swaziland · Public history DB · Leanings: South African nonprofit history DB, anti-apartheid and liberation movement perspective — https://www.sahistory.org.za/place/swaziland

Suppression of the Manzini Democracy Protest on April 12, 2011 Protest · 2011

According to Mail & Guardian (Sapa-AFP, 2011-04-12), approximately 1,000 teachers and students marched to Manzini to join a democracy protest against King Mswati III that the authorities had banned, but were blocked by police tear gas and water cannons. When protesters gathered outside the Swaziland National Association of Teachers office on the outskirts of the city and erected barricades, police entered the building, and the teachers' association reported that police were beating teachers. Earlier on the same day, dozens of activists, including union leaders Muzi Nhlangula and Sithabile Majozi, had been arrested. Protesters demanded political participation under the absolute monarchy, while authorities treated the protest as an unlawful march.

2021 Pro-Democracy and Anti-Police Violence Protests and Riots, 2023 Assassination of Tabane Maseko Uprising · 2021–2023

According to Amnesty International (2021-11-16), following the discovery on May 14 of law student Thabani Nkomonye (25) dead, protests demanding an end to police violence spread from a local constituency. On June 25, the acting prime minister issued a proclamation banning all protests and petition deliveries, and security forces began crackdowns. Violent unrest broke out nationwide from June 28 to July 4, internet was shut down on June 29, and a Southern African Development Community (SADC) investigation team arrived on July 4. On July 16, the king announced Cleopas Dlamini as the new prime minister, and on July 25, two lawmakers were arrested on charges including the Terrorism Suppression Act. On October 1, more than 10,000 people marched to the US embassy, internet was shut down again on October 15, and nationwide protests were overreactively suppressed on October 18. On the government side, Deputy Minister of State Manko Kubisho told AFP that 'it was not protest but looting, arson, and destruction' and alleged foreign involvement (ECR), while the UN Human Rights Office raised concerns about disproportionate use of force by security forces. On January 21, 2023, Thulani Maseko, a human rights lawyer representing two lawmakers in the 2021 unrest-related trial and president of the Dialogue 4 Change Forum, was shot dead at his home in Manzini; on January 23, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk called for a swift and independent investigation (UN News). The government describes the events as restoring order and protecting property, while protesters and human rights organizations characterize them as repression of demands for political reform.

2. Before the Industrial Revolution (~1759) — Records of Uprisings and Peasant Wars

Expulsion of Portuguese forces by King Mavumengwana in 1674 Mutapa Kingdom · 1674

According to the South African History Online (SAHO) Zimbabwe entry, the Mutapa Kingdom was founded around 1430 by Nyatsimba Mutota, and the Portuguese sought to control inland resources from the 1600s onward. In 1674, King Mavumengwana expelled the Portuguese from their forts and farms. From the Mutapa perspective, it was resistance against foreign interference in internal affairs; in Portuguese records, it was an event that led to the loss of a trading outpost.

  1. South African History Online — Zimbabwe · Public history DB · Affiliation: South African nonprofit history DB, anti-colonial/liberation movement perspective — https://www.sahistory.org.za/place/zimbabwe

Changamire Dombo's rebellion and the founding of the Rozwi Kingdom (1684 Mahungwe, 1693 Dambare) End of Mutapa Kingdom ~ Founding of Rozwi Kingdom · 1670–1695

According to the SAHO entry, Changa Murembwa Dombo rebelled between 1670 and 1690 to establish the Rozwi Kingdom, defeating Portuguese forces at Mahungwe in 1684 and at Dambare in 1693. By around 1695, the Rozwi Kingdom had become the premier kingdom of the region, replacing Mutapa. Dombo's uprising is described as an act of secession within the Mutapa monarchy that also involved armed resistance against Portuguese power.

  1. South African History Online — Zimbabwe · Public history DB · Orientation: South African nonprofit history DB, anti-colonial/liberation movement perspective — https://www.sahistory.org.za/place/zimbabwe

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

First Chiminuka (1896–1897) — Ndebele and Shona Uprising Uprising · 1896–1897

According to the SAHO Zimbabwe entry, the Ndebele entered the region under Gundwane's leadership in 1838–39 and subsequently came under the rule of Mzilikazi. The British South Africa Company (BSAC) was chartered in 1889. In March 1896, the Ndebele rebelled against company rule, followed by the Shona in June. Zimbabwean nationalist narratives describe this as the First Chimurenga (Liberation Struggle), while company and colonial records characterize it as a native rebellion. The SAHO entry does not report casualty figures.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other

Data Record: Zimbabwe (Rhodesia) is absent from the entries of COW, UCDP, and NAVCO (the colonial period; not a state in the COW system).

  1. South African History Online — Zimbabwe · Public history database · Orientation: South African nonprofit history database, anti-colonial/liberation movement perspective — https://www.sahistory.org.za/place/zimbabwe

1965 Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) and the 1966–1979 Liberation War (Second Chimurenga) Civil war · 1965–1980

According to the SAHO entry, in 1965 the Ian Smith government unilaterally declared independence from Britain under white minority rule, and full-scale hostilities began in 1966. In 1977–78, more than 1,000 Mozambican Zimbabwean refugees were killed by Rhodesian forces, and ZIPRA shot down two civilian aircraft in 1978 and 1979, killing a total of 107 people. The Lancaster House Agreement was signed on December 21, 1979, and ZANU won the February 1980 elections, with Robert Mugabe becoming the first Prime Minister. The Rhodesian government described this as counter-terrorism, while ZANU and ZAPU portrayed it as a liberation war for majority rule.

NAVCO 1.3 records the ZAPU campaign (1972–1979) as violent and partially successful. The COW civil war data do not include the Rhodesian War under the Zimbabwe entry.

Gukurahundi in Matabeleland and Midlands, 1982–1987 Civil war · 1982–1987

The SAHO entry states that killings known as Gukurahundi continued until 1987, with approximately 20,000 civilians killed, most of them at the hands of government forces. The government at the time described this as an operation to suppress ZAPU-aligned 'anti-government elements,' while residents of affected areas and human rights organizations describe it as a massacre targeting Ndebele-speaking civilians.

NAVCO 1.3 records the 'PF-ZAPU guerrillas' (1983–1987) as a violence and partial success campaign against the Mugabe government, capturing an event centered on civilian casualties within a framework of anti-government campaigns only. ACLED begins counting from 1997.

Political Violence Surrounding the 2008 Presidential Runoff Protests · 2008

According to Human Rights Watch's report 'Bullets for Each of You' (2008-06-08), the results of the March 29 general election and first round of presidential voting were announced on May 2, with Morgan Tsvangirai at 47.9% and Robert Mugabe at 43.2%, and the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission scheduled the runoff for June 27. The report states that by May 27 at least 36 people had been killed, local institutions had confirmed at least 2,000 cases of beatings and torture, and more than 3,000 people had become internally displaced. HRW describes the violence as primarily perpetrated by ZANU-PF affiliates and 'veterans' and youth militias with military, police, correctional services, and CIO support, coordinated by the Joint Operations Command. The government portrayed the violence reports as exaggerations mainly attributable to the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), and the military denied involvement in a May 8 statement. The SAHO entry notes that ZANU-PF lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in this election.

Military Intervention and Mugabe's Resignation in November 2017 Coup · 2017

According to Reuters (reprinted by Daily Star, 2017-11-21), that month President Mugabe dismissed Vice President Mnangagwa to clear the way for his wife Grace Mugabe's accession to power, and this dismissal triggered the military takeover. Mnangagwa left the country out of fear for his safety. After the military takeover, Mugabe stayed virtually in Harare's official residence for about a week, was ousted from ZANU-PF, and thousands held anti-Mugabe rallies. Immediately after parliament began impeachment proceedings on November 21, Jacob Mudenda, the speaker, read his letter of resignation at a joint meeting, bringing to an end 37 years in power. The article does not report casualties for this period, and how the military and Mugabe's side characterized the event are not stated in this article (unverified).

NAVCO 1.3 records the 'anti-Mugabe' campaign (2016–2017) as nonviolent and successful, attributing the same exit to the coup data as a military action and to the campaign data as a success of the civil movement.

Shooting of Protesters over Election Results in Harare on August 1, 2018 Protest · 2018–2019

According to the South African Institute for Security Studies (ISS Today, Derek Matyszak, 2019-08-12), on August 1, 2018, the military fired live ammunition into protests in central Harare against election results, killing six civilians. The troops were commanded by Major General Anselem Nainda Sanyatwe, and the author attributes the decision to deploy them to Defense Minister Constantino Chiwenga. A seven-member commission appointed by President Mnangagwa (chairman: former South African president Thabo Mbeki; four members foreign nationals) found that the protests had been pre-planned by the MDC Alliance (MDC-A) and that the deployment of troops met constitutional requirements, recommended prosecuting protesters for property destruction, and recommended handling soldiers who killed civilians through internal military 'disciplinary' procedures. The author criticizes the commission's conclusion as standing on a void of evidence. As of August 2019, the recommended disciplinary action against the soldiers had not been implemented, and the United States imposed a travel ban on Sanyatwe.

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

The 1955 Torit Rebellion and the First Sudanese Civil War (Anyanya, 1955–1972) Civil War · 1955–1972

According to a submission by Radio Tamazuj (2024-03-21), on August 18, 1955, a mutiny broke out in Torit led by southern soldiers of the Equatoria Corps, and the rebellion spread to Juba, Yei, Yambio, and Maridi. In 1963, southern rebel factions united under the Anyanya movement, and the Sudanese Liberation Movement (SSLM) became a political organization. The war ended with the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement, which guaranteed autonomy for the southern regions. The SSLM and Anyanya delegations were led by Ezbon Mondiri in negotiations, while the government delegation was led by Abel Alier. The Khartoum central government describes it as a military mutiny and separatist armed activity, whereas the southern side describes it as resistance demanding representation and autonomy. The submission is presented as an opinion piece by a graduate student author.

Total deaths in the First Civil WarUnconfirmedUnverified (not found on the year page)

Data Record: The COW, UCDP, and NAVCO entries for South Sudan (SSD) cover only the period after independence in 2011. This war is an event in the Sudan (SDN) entry and does not appear in this country's data table.

The 1983 Bor Mutiny and the Second Sudanese Civil War (SPLM/A, 1983–2005) Civil War · 1983–2005

According to a Radio Tamale article (2024), on May 16, 1983, a mutiny broke out in Bole's 105th Battalion near Bor Malual Chut, led by a Kerubino Kwan Yinin; at the same time, the 104th Battalion mutinied in Ayod. Colonel John Garang, sent to persuade the mutineers, joined them and became chairman and commander-in-chief of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement/Army (SPLM/A) in June 1983. The war ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA), signed in Kenya on January 9, 2005; Garang died in a helicopter crash on July 30 of the same year. The CPA set a timetable for a referendum on southern independence (University of Notre Dame peace agreement matrix). The Sudanese government describes it as a suppression of rebels, while the SPLM/A describes it as a liberation struggle for 'New Sudan' and southern rights.

2011 Independence Referendum Regime Overthrow · 2011

According to the Notre Dame Peace Agreement Matrix, the Southern Sudan independence referendum was held from January 9–15, 2011, and the Southern Sudan Referendum Commission announced on February 7 that 98.83% of valid votes favored secession and 1.17% favored unity, with a turnout of 97.58% (3,851,994 registered voters). Al Jazeera (2011-02-07) reported that the vote for unity was 44,888 votes, and President Omar al-Bashir stated on state TV that he accepted the results. The Abyei referendum was not held because an agreement on voter eligibility could not be reached. South Sudan became independent on July 9, 2011. This entry is not a forcible overthrow of the regime but a secession in accordance with an agreement; it is classified under the 'regime overthrow' category to align with the Series classification.

The December 2013 Juba Crisis and the South Sudan Civil War (2013–2018) Civil War · 2013–2018

According to the final report of the African Union Commission on South Sudan (AUCISS) reported by Radio Tamazuj (2015-10-27), an internal shootout within the presidential guard in December 2013 triggered Dinka guards and security forces to target Nuer soldiers and civilians in Juba, and the commission found that killings were 'widespread and systematic' and possibly coordinated and planned according to state policy. The commission stated that it found no evidence of a coup attempt as claimed by President Salva Kiir. The report documented the killing of approximately 90 Nuer civilians and 21 demobilized soldiers at J2 Palace and approximately 134 Nuer men at the Gudele Joint Operations Centre. The government describes the conflict as a coup attempt by the Machar faction, while the rebels (SPLM-IO) and the commission describe it as an escalation of the civil war from targeted killings. According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS, 2018-09-28), a new peace agreement (the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan, R-ARCSS) was signed on September 12, and about 4.5 million people had been displaced by the war. In Juba from July 7 to 11, 2016, forces loyal to both Kiir and Machar clashed again, and Amnesty International (2016-10-24) reported that government forces deliberately killed Nuer civilians and committed large-scale looting.

Nasir clashes and the detention of Riek Machar in 2025Civil War · 2025

According to The EastAfrican (2025-03-27), which published a Reuters article, fighting broke out in Nasir, Upper Nile State, in early March between government forces and the 'White Army,' mainly Nuer youth, and the Kiir government detained several SPLM-IO officials including the oil minister and deputy chief of defense staff. SPLM-IO stated that security officials with arrest warrants forcibly entered Machar's residence in Juba, and Machar was reported to be under house arrest along with his wife and two bodyguards. SPLM-IO denied current links to the White Army. UNMISS warned leaders that they were 'on the brink of a widespread conflict' and urged restraint, while the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of African Affairs demanded the measures be withdrawn. Government and military spokespersons did not respond to requests for comment.

5. Modern Events through the Literature

1959–1961 Hutu 'Social Revolution'Uprising · 1959–1961

According to the UN Rwanda Genocide Outreach Programme, a violent incident in November 1959 triggered a Hutu uprising that killed hundreds of Tutsi and left thousands homeless; this 'Hutu Peasant Revolution' continued from 1959 to 1961. By the time of independence in 1962, approximately 120,000 people, mostly Tutsi, had fled to neighboring countries. The Mémorial de la Shoah chronology describes the same event as a 'Hutu social revolution' in which hundreds of Tutsi were killed and tens of thousands went into exile. Hutu political parties describe it as a social revolution against the monarchy and the Tutsi elite, while exiled Tutsi and subsequent genocide studies describe it as the starting point of violence targeting Tutsi.

1963–1964 Exile Tutsi Armed Attacks and Retaliatory Massacres Civil War · 1963–1964

According to the UN outreach programme, exiled Tutsi refugees launched ten attacks between 1962 and 1967, followed each time by retaliatory killings of Tutsi civilians inside Rwanda. The Shoah Memorial chronology states that in December 1963–January 1964, the Kigoma region lost 10–20% of its Tutsi population; violence spread along surrounding roads, killing 10,000–14,000 people and displacing tens of thousands more. The government side describes it as defense against an invasion by armed exiles (Inyenzi), while some Tutsi and researchers describe it as a massacre of civilians.

1973 Purge and Habyarimana Coup Coup · 1973

According to the Shoah Memorial chronology, approximately 200 people were killed in a purge targeting Tutsi in February–March 1973. On July 5, 1973, Juvénal Habyarimana overthrew the government of Grégoire Kayibanda (Powell & Thyne coup data · Archigos record). Narrative sources on the circumstances of the coup could not be found in the pages consulted for this round, so only dataset records are noted.

1990–1994 Civil War and 1994 Tutsi Genocide Civil War · 1990–1994

According to the UN outreach programme, by the late 1980s there were approximately 480,000 Rwandan refugees, and the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) was founded in Kampala, Uganda, in 1988. On October 1, 1990, the RPF attacked Rwanda from Uganda with a force of approximately 7,000 troops. The Arusha Peace Accords were signed in August 1993, and the UN Security Council established the United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda (UNAMIR) in October. Massacres began after the crash of the presidential plane on April 6, 1994; on April 7, Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana and ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed. On April 21, UNAMIR troop numbers fell from 2,165 to 270. The RPF militarily took control of the country on July 4. The Shoah Memorial chronology notes that by July 19 more than 2 million Hutu civilians had been driven into Zaire and Tanzania. Immediately after the RPF attack in October 1990, thousands of people, mostly Tutsi, were imprisoned on suspicion of conspiracy (Shoah Memorial). The Rwandan government and the UN officially characterize it as 'genocide against the Tutsi'; accounts of the death toll differ between government tallies and independent research.

Women rapedUnconfirmed150,000–250,000 (UN outreach programme) / 250,000–500,000 (Survivors Fund, citing Foundation Rwanda 2019)

The 1,000 combat deaths in COW and the genocide fatalities (800,000–1,074,017) have entirely different definitions. Powell & Thyne record the 1994-04-07 coup as a successful one; Archigos records Habyarimana's departure as irregular and fatal.

2. Pre-Industrial Revolution (~1759) — Records of Uprisings and Civil War

Attack on the Fort-Dauphin colonial outpost and the end of the first French colonization Modern · 1643–1674

In 1643, the French East India Company established its first colonial outpost at Fort-Dauphin in the southern Antanosy region of the island, using it as a base for expeditions to Bourbon (now Réunion). On August 27, 1674, local inhabitants attacked the colonists, killing many; Fort-Dauphin was abandoned after the incident, and the survivors moved to Bourbon. The consulted sources did not specify the direct cause of the attack or the number of fatalities. For uprisings and civil wars among the inland kingdoms of Madagascar during this period, no public records were found in this survey and are therefore omitted.

5. Modern Events in the Literature

1947 Madagascar Uprising (Anti-Colonial Armed Uprising) Uprising · 1947–1949

The uprising began on the night of March 29, 1947, when two secret societies simultaneously attacked French colonial authorities across several parts of the island. Earlier, in March 1946, MDRM lawmakers Ratsimandresy and Rabearivelo had submitted a bill for independence within the French Union; parliament refused even to print it and rejected it, and in the November 1946 elections all three seats reserved for indigenous people went to MDRM leaders. The French government chose repression over negotiation, and the war ended roughly two years later. Estimates of the death toll vary widely across sources (see figures). UCDP records this event as a territorial dispute between the French government and the MDRM (a colonial external conflict), with 1,000+ deaths in 1947 alone constituting a year of war. In 2025, reports emerged that Z-generation protesters had sung MDRM songs again.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Deaths (official French government announcement at the time)Over 100,000 (Madagascar High Commissioner) / approximately 8,000 (cited in the French National Assembly at the time)Fremigacci: up to approximately 10,000 killed during the uprising (including 140 whites) + estimated 20,000–30,000 excess deaths from malnutrition and disease in uprising-affected areas
Deaths (historian estimates, 2026 reports)10,000–40,000 killed in the repression (estimates by historians cited by allAfrica)

Data Record: Recorded as UCDP Conflict 219 (1947, colonial external/territorial), but the end year is recorded only as 1947, differing from the narrative sources' report of a 'roughly two-year' duration (ending around 1949). Not listed in the COW civil war list.

  2. Madagascar: Gen Z members commemorate the 79th anniversary of an anti-colonial uprising — allAfrica (2026) · Media — https://fr.allafrica.com/stories/202604060111.html

Southern Toliara Farmers' Uprising (Monima) Uprising · 1971

In April 1971, the Movement of National Independence of Madagascar (Monima) led a farmers' uprising in the Toliara region. After the suppression, Monima was dissolved and its leaders, including Moneza Joana, were exiled to Nosy Lava. Estimates of fatalities range widely from 50 to 1,000.

May 1972 Student and Urban Protests (Rotaka) and the Fall of the Chirananana Government Regime Overthrow · 1972

President Chirananana took office for a third term (a seventh-year term) on January 30, 1972, but students at the University of Antananarivo resisted his authority for more than three weeks. On May 12–13, authorities arrested hundreds of student leaders and sent them to Nosy Lava; on May 13, the Republican Security Force (FRS) fired on protesters, killing 15–40 people and wounding approximately 150. The protests were confined to the capital, where the city hall building was burned. On May 18, Chirananana dissolved the government and transferred full authority to the armed forces under General Ramanantsoa, effectively bringing the First Republic to an end.

Assassination of President Ratsimandrava and Seizure of Power by Military Leadership Coup · 1975

On February 5, 1975, General Ramanantsoa transferred power to Captain Richard Ratsimandrava; five days later, Ratsimandrava was assassinated. The High Command of the National Armed Forces then took power, and on June 15 it elected Commander Didier Ratsiraka as head of state and president of the High Revolutionary Council.

Data Record: Archigos records Ramanantsoa's departure as 'an internal military power struggle that did not lead to a coup' and Ratsimandrava's departure as 'removal by the military (killed).' The Powell & Thyne list contains only the failed coup of December 31, 1974; the assassination in February 1975 was not separately coded as a coup.

The 1991 Democratic General Strike and the Shooting at Iavoloha's 'March for Freedom' Protest · 1991–1993

In May 1991, a coalition of 16 opposition parties and social organizations called 'Forces Vives' (led by Albert Zafy) organized the first large-scale general strike; in July, a state of emergency was declared following protests in the capital attended by approximately 400,000 people. On August 10, protesters demanding President Ratsiraka's resignation marched on Iavoloha Palace with a 'March for Freedom,' and presidential guards opened fire on the crowd. General strikes continued throughout August, and the Council of Christian Churches sided with the protesters. On October 31, Ratsiraka agreed to a new constitution and multiparty elections; the new constitution was approved in August 1992, and Zafy won the runoff in February 1993 with 67% of the vote. Ratsiraka returned to power in the 1997 election.

2001 Presidential Election Dispute and 2002 Dual Government Crisis Regime Overthrow · 2002

Following the December 16, 2001 presidential election, Ravalomanana claimed victory with a first-round majority, while Ratsiraka, who had ruled for 20 years, demanded a runoff on the grounds that no candidate had won a majority. Ravalomanana called a general strike in January and inaugurated his cabinet at its peak. Ratsiraka retreated to his stronghold of Antsirabe, imposing a blockade on the capital; food and fuel from the port were cut off, and attempts to use other ports were thwarted by the destruction of a bridge. Reports indicated that retaliatory violence between supporters of the two sides left fatalities and approximately 100,000 jobs lost. Mediation by the UN, OAU, and Indian Ocean Commission yielded no results by April. Ratsiraka left the country in July 2002.

2009 Political Crisis — Ambohitsorohitra Firing and Transfer of Power in March Coup · 2008–2009

From late 2008, unrest continued amid a confrontation between the camps of President Ravalomanana and Mayor Rajoelina of Antananarivo. On February 7, 2009, the presidential guard fired live rounds into an unarmed opposition protest marching toward Ambohitsorohitra (the presidential palace), killing at least 31 according to Amnesty International's tally. Dozens were also reported killed in January unrest. On March 17, military commanders to whom Ravalomanana had transferred power handed it over to Rajoelina, who took power. Amnesty recorded that no independent investigation had taken place.

November 2010 Military Coup Attempt Coup · 2010

On November 17, 2010, the day a referendum on a new constitution proposed by Rajoelina was held, a group of officers gathered at a base near Antananarivo airport and declared their seizure of power. The vote proceeded as planned. Reports reviewed did not record casualties from this attempt.

Data Record: Consistent with Powell & Thyne's 2010-11-17 failed coup.

  1. Madagascan coup attempt fizzling — Mail & Guardian (2010-11-19) · Media — https://mg.co.za/article/2010-11-19-madagascan-coup-attempt-fizzling

2025 Z-Generation Protests and CAPSAT Military Seizure of Power Coup · 2025

On September 25, 2025, youth-led protests against frequent water and power outages in the capital began, and the agenda later broadened to include poverty and corruption issues. The president dismissed the government and appointed an army general as prime minister, but protesters rejected the offer of dialogue. On October 11 (Saturday), a CAPSAT unit led by Captain Randrianirina sided with the protesters; President Rajoelina left the country citing threats to his safety, and parliament impeached him. Randrianirina seized power on October 14, and the African Union suspended Madagascar's membership. He stated he would be inaugurated at the High Constitutional Court on October 17 and promised elections within two years. Rajoelina refused to recognize this seizure of power and rejected resignation.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

Chilembwe Rising Uprising · 1915

Reverend John Chilembwe, who had been educated in the United States and returned to Nyasaland (Malawi) in 1900 to lead the Providence Industrial Mission, led a brief armed uprising in British-ruled Nyasaland in 1915. The largest attack was on January 23 (Saturday), when a raid was launched against the headquarters of the 163,000-acre Magomero Farm, run by Alexander Livingstone Bruce, grandson of David Livingstone; William Jarvis Livingston, the farm manager, was killed, and three Europeans died in total, including in attacks on outlying sites. Subsequently, an attack was launched against the African Lakes Company headquarters in Blantyre (Mandalira) to obtain weapons, and small-scale attacks occurred in Zomba, Chinthu, and Mulanje but did not spread. The uprising ended within days, after which approximately 30 people were executed and many more were imprisoned for long terms. Participants who had been former capataes (foremen) at Magomero Farm testified to grievances over treatment, including flogging, and the prohibition on building schools and churches on the farm. The Malawian government today honors Chilembwe as the first 'original' nationalist, featuring his portrait on banknotes.

Nyasaland African Congress and the 1959 State of Emergency Protests · 1958–1959

In 1958, the Nyasaland African Congress (NAC), led by Hastings Banda, began a nonviolent campaign against the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, including tax refusal. In 1959, the British and Nyasaland governments declared a state of emergency on the basis of intelligence alleging that the NAC had plotted to destroy and kill. During the suppression, approximately 1,300 Africans were detained and 51 died. The Deverell Commission, appointed by the British government, reported on July 16, 1959, rejecting evidence of a 'murder plot' and criticizing the handling of the emergency, characterizing Nyasaland as a 'police state,' and confirming African opposition to the federation. In the same month, the Monkton Commission was established to review the federation. Murphy (2010), based on declassified Colonial Office documents, analyzed that intelligence and security officials were more cautious about the information than Conservative ministers.

The 1992 Bishops' Pastoral Letter and the Dissolution of Banda's One-Party Regime Protests · 1992–1994

On March 8, 1992, the Catholic Bishops' Conference of Malawi issued a Lenten pastoral letter criticizing the government's human rights record and social policies. Amnesty International recorded this as the first public criticism of the Banda administration since the 1960s. The bishops were interrogated by police for eight hours; the letter was designated an inciting publication; at a meeting of the ruling Malawi Congress Party, calls to execute the bishops were broadcast on radio; and the Balaka printing works that had printed the letter were firebombed. On April 6, labor activists Chakufwa Chihana and Chihana were arrested upon their return from abroad at the airport. Subsequently, there are recollections of violent strikes in Blantyre and Lilongwe in which more than 60 people died from gunfire. Banda announced a referendum for October of that year; in the June 14, 1993 referendum, multipartyism was chosen; and general elections were held in 1994.

Bloody Crackdown on Anti-Government Protests, July 20, 2011 Protest · 2011–2012

On July 20, 2011, protests against deteriorating economic conditions and intensifying repression were held in Lilongwe, Blantyre, and Zomba. Police fired live ammunition and tear gas at unarmed protesters and passersby, killing 19 and injuring dozens, with approximately 500 arrested. The broadcasting regulatory body ordered three private radio stations to cease live broadcasts on the same day. President Mutharika promised an independent investigation on August 10, but it had not been established by the time of the Human Rights Watch report. The UK withheld $30 million in aid in July, and the US announced a suspension of $350 million in support on July 26.

The 2019 Presidential Election 'Tepezha' Dispute and the 2020 Re-election Protest · 2019–2020

Following President Mutharika's narrow victory declaration in the May 2019 presidential election, the Human Rights Defenders Coalition led nationwide protests demanding a fair election. On February 3, 2020, the Constitutional Court annulled the results citing evidence of fraud, including thousands of tally sheets that appeared to have been altered (Tepezha), and the Supreme Court upheld this decision. The day before the rerun election, clashes broke out in Lilongwe and Nkhotakota over rumors of ballot tampering, and the Malawi Defense Force restored order. A rerun election was held on June 23, 2020, in which opposition MCP leader Lazarus Chakwera faced incumbent Mutharika.

2. Before the Industrial Revolution (~1759) — Records of Uprisings and Peasant Wars

Armed resistance by Maroons (runaway slaves) Early French rule in Île de France · 1722–1732

Mauritius had no indigenous population; from the Dutch occupation of the 17th century onward, African and Malagasy slaves brought to the island fled into the forests to form 'Maroon' (marron) communities. Historian Satyendra Peerthum (contributing to Le Mauricien) dates Maroon activity in colonial Mauritius to 1641–1839. In December 1721, French colonists arrived at Port Louis with slaves from Bourbon (Réunion), and in December 8, 1722, 65 slaves arriving on the Le Rubis fled into the forest within days, apparently joining Maroons left behind by the Dutch. On November 12, 1723, the local council sentenced three habitual runaways to death by drawing lots; Peerthum records this as the first conviction handed down to a Maroon on the island. On March 24, 1724, an armed group of Maroons seized a military post in the Savanne district and drove off the soldiers. A council proclamation of June 2, 1726 established armed bands to track Maroons, transferring captured Maroons to the trackers' ownership (with 2–3 executed) and offering 100 livres for the left hand of a Maroon killed in combat. In 1732, a group of Maroons attacked a post and settlement at Plaisance (Flacq), killing 10 French and several settlers while losing one Maroon, according to Peerthum, citing Governor La Bourdonnaye's records. The French authorities regained control in the late 1730s and early 1740s during La Bourdonnaye's governorship. This account centers on slave resistance as written by a scholar; colonial authorities at the time treated it as a security threat.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

Violence Surrounding the 1911 General Election Protest · 1911

In 1911, violence broke out between the 'Action Libérale' led by Dr. Eugène Laurent in Quiripif and Port-Louis and the 'oligarchic' forces based among white farmers. The commission of inquiry established by Governor Cavendish Boyle attributed the causes to the oligarchs' attack on Laurent, rumors of Laurent's assassination, and the inefficiency of the police. Le Mauricien notes that British troops (mostly Sikh soldiers) were deployed but did not need to use their weapons. The number of casualties does not appear in sources checked.

1937 Sugarcane Plantation Unrest (Uba Unrest) Protest · 1937

In August 1937, a strike broke out at a sugarcane plantation in Mauritius, leading to clashes between the plantation manager and temporary workers, resulting in the deaths of four men (abstract of Hurgobin's AHA 2017 presentation). Workers were dissatisfied with low wages and the plantation's recruitment practices, and the strike spread to other plantations across the island. The colonial government established a commission of inquiry to investigate the unrest, and the Imperial Indian Citizenship Association in Bombay requested the Indian government to look into the treatment of temporary workers. The names of the plantation (Union Flax) and the committee (Hopper Committee) were not confirmed in academic sources consulted for this round.

Belle Vue Harel Shooting Incident Protest · 1943

On September 13, 1943, workers at the Belle Vue Harel sugarcane plantation went on strike. Around 10–11 AM on September 27 (Monday), approximately 200 to 300 men, women, and children armed with sticks and stones clashed with police, who fired 16 shots. Anjalay Coopen (recorded as pregnant at age 32), Kistnasami Muniyam, and Manseem Muniend died, and Marde Panapen died nine days later at the Port-Louis General Hospital. There were five gunshot victims and twelve injured (Parsuramen & Peerthum, Le Mauricien). The authors cite records from the National Archives and a 1943 October document from the Governor's Public Relations Office, but the conclusion of that document was not cited in the article. Anjalay Coopen is subsequently commemorated as a symbol of the Mauritian labor movement.

Inter-Community Conflict in Port Louis Immediately Before Independence Uprising · 1968

Communal clashes broke out in the eastern suburbs of Port Louis a few weeks before independence (March 12, 1968). Le Mauricien (2022) describes this as 'racial riots' in February, and reports that independent media had reported 14 deaths by February 9, 1968. The KSLI, a British Army battalion, was dispatched from Malaysia to Mauritius without prior notice under the command of Major Brian Lowe. The start date of the clashes, the date of the state of emergency declaration, and the final death toll could not be confirmed from sources consulted for this round. Accounts from each community were not separately cited from verified sources.

Kaya's Death and the February 1999 Riots Uprising · 1999

In February 1999, popular Creole singer Kaya died while in police custody. According to the U.S. Department of State Country Reports on Human Rights Practices (2000 edition), his death led to three days of riots during which police shot and killed three protesters and a policeman died of a heart attack. Shops, houses, and churches were burned and looted, with damages estimated at approximately $50 million (1.25 billion rupees). Following a second investigation into the shooting death of another Creole musician during the riots, the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) recommended disciplinary proceedings against three police officers in May 2000. In October 2000, the government released the report of the Judicial Inquiry Commission on the riots. The report criticized previous governments and the police for their handling of the riots and also criticized some opposition politicians and Creole activists for inciting some of the rioting. Although the commission did not investigate Kaya's death itself, it criticized the excessive use of high-security detention for him given the nature of the allegations against him. Investigations into Kaya's death continued through late 2000, and no action was taken on the deaths during the riots. The police established an Internal Complaints Bureau (CIB) in October 1999.

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

Mueda Plateau Shooting Protest · 1960

On June 16, 1960, the Governor of Cabo Delgado held a meeting with Mueda Plateau representatives linked to the Mozambique African Alliance (MAA-SAM). According to the description at the Aljube Museum in Lisbon, the agenda included the return of Makonde people who had remained in Tanganyika and demands for labor conditions, land use, and the abolition of forced labor; independence and nationalism were not the main issues. When the governor ordered the arrest of the representatives, intense reactions broke out among thousands of attendees, and people died from colonial authorities' gunfire; some died after being crushed while fleeing in disorder. The number of deaths has never been definitively established: Portuguese authorities reported 14, direct witnesses reported 16, FRELIMO (an estimate five years later) reported 150, and some sources report 600. Portugal remembers it as the suppression of unrest, while Mozambique's narrative recalls it as a colonial massacre.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
Deaths14 (Portuguese authorities' report — cited by the Aljube Museum)16 (direct witnesses) / 150 (FRELIMO estimate around 1965) / 600 (some sources)

Data Record: Not included in the modern dataset (UCDP's Portuguese–FRELIMO conflict starts in 1964). NAVCO codes the FRELIMO campaign as 1962–1975.

FRELIMO–RENAMO Civil War and the General Peace Agreement of Rome Civil War · 1977–1992

Mozambique, which had gained independence from Portugal in 1975, entered a protracted civil war between the FRELIMO government and RENAMO. Canadian Department of National Defence military history materials state that RENAMO was formed with assistance from Rhodesia in 1976, while UN peacekeeping materials indicate that the apartheid South African regime supported RENAMO. After two years of negotiations, a General Peace Agreement was signed in Rome on October 4, 1992. The Security Council established the United Nations Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ) by Resolution 797 (1992) on December 16, 1992, and under Special Representative Aldo Ajello approximately 6,500 troops and military observers were deployed early in 1993. More than 76,000 troops from both sides were demobilized, about 10,000 were integrated into the new national army, and approximately 155,000 weapons were recovered. In the first multiparty elections in October 1994, FRELIMO won both the parliamentary and presidential elections. The government side has described this war as an 'instability war' sponsored by external powers (Rhodesia and South Africa), while the RENAMO side has described it as an armed struggle against the one-party system.

Maputo Bread Price Riots Protest · 2010

On September 1, 2010, when bread prices rose by approximately 22%, a campaign urging protests via mobile text messages and email spread, and clashes broke out between police and protesters in Maputo and nearby Matola. According to SADOCC (Southern African Documentation and Cooperation Centre, 9.8) compilation, 13 people were killed, 175 injured, and the police arrested 286 people. Sixty-six stores were looted, and damage was estimated at approximately 24 million rand (provisional). Protests also occurred in Chimoio, and small-scale protests in Beira, Tete, and Nampula were suppressed. The government initially stated that the price increase could not be reversed, but Planning and Development Minister Armando Emílio Guebuza announced a reduction in bread prices through subsidies, a 7.5% reduction in rice prices, a temporary suspension of sugar imports, a freeze on salaries for high-ranking public officials and state enterprise representatives, and cuts in public spending (Sapa wire).

Cabala Armed Rebellion Civil War · 2017–

Following the first attack in the Mocímboa da Praia district of Cabo Delgado province on October 5, 2017, northern armed rebellion continued. ACLED tallies (reported by RTP; up to late November of an unspecified year — article publication year not indicated) recorded 2,270 violent events since October 2017, of which 2,107 involved 'Islamic State in Mozambique' (EIM), with 6,341 deaths. The same report also conveyed the spread to the Mambu and Erati districts of neighboring Nampula province and 21 civilian deaths in those areas. The government has characterized this as terrorism and responded accordingly; no official account from armed forces is found in sources consulted.

Post-2024 Presidential Election Protests and Crackdowns Protest · 2024–2025

Following Daniel Chambal's announcement as the winner of the October 9, 2024 presidential election, protests began at the urging of Benjamim Mondlane, the second-place opposition candidate. On October 18, two opposition figures were shot and killed in their vehicle by unknown assailants, which their party called a political assassination. According to AP (2024.12.12), civil society election monitoring group Plataforma Decide tallied 110 deaths since October 21 (34 between December 4 and 10), and Amnesty International cited the same figure while reporting 357 victims of security force shootings and over 3,500 arbitrary arrests. The authorities stated that the protests turned violent and suppression was inevitable, and the military was deployed. The military said a video showing a military vehicle striking female protesters was an accident. International election observation missions reported electoral fraud. Mondlane, who left the country citing threats to his safety, continued to urge protests via social media.
