5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

October 1965 Coup Attempt and Execution of Hutu Politicians Coup · 1965

In the first national assembly elections after independence in May 1965, Hutu candidates won 23 of 33 seats, but the king appointed a non-Hutu royal confidant, Léopold Bihamwabani, as prime minister. On October 18, 1965, Hutu forces attempted a coup targeting the royal palace, followed by sporadic attacks against Tutsi in the interior. The king fled abroad and did not return. In retaliation, Tutsi units of the army and gendarmerie arrested and executed 86 leading Hutu politicians and officers (Lemarchand).

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations · Other
Hutu Politicians and Officers Executed in RetaliationNo government figures in confirmed data86 (Lemarchand 2009)

Data Record: Powell & Thyne records the October 18, 1965 attempt as a 'failed' coup. The two successful coups of July and November 1966 (deposing Ntare V and Ntaré IV) appear in the P&T and Archigos tables.

  1. René Lemarchand, 'The Burundi Genocide', in Totten & Parsons (eds.), Century of Genocide, 3rd ed. (Routledge 2009) — Publisher-provided chapter PDF · Academic monograph (chapter) · Orientation: genocide studies perspective; the author characterizes the 1972 event as genocide — https://asset.routledge.com/rt-media/pdf/9780415871921/chapter10_theburundi_genocide.pdf

The 1972 Hutu Uprising and Ikyza (Massacre) Uprising · 1972

On April 29, 1972, armed uprisings led by Hutu broke out in the southern lakeside cities of Rumonge and Nyanza-Lac, resulting in massacres of Tutsi residents within hours. The military of the Mwimba government (mostly Tutsi) responded with large-scale massacres targeting Hutu, especially educated Hutu elites, from May through July–August. Lemarchand conservatively estimates 100,000 to 150,000 deaths in one passage and 200,000 to 300,000 in another; the opposition Hutu side claimed 300,000, while the first figure given by Burundian authorities was 15,000. He describes that the government did not conduct a serious investigation into the scale and that the 1972 events have been erased from official Burundian memory today. Surface calm continued until 1988 amid a vacuum of Hutu elite leadership.

Hutu Fatalities15,000 (first figure released by Burundian authorities, cited by Lemarchand)Conservative estimates of 100,000 to 150,000 and accounts stating 200,000 to 300,000 also noted (Lemarchand 2009); opposition Hutu side claimed 300,000

Data Record: COW records only the 'First Burundi War of 1972' (combat deaths: 1,000) — killings of unarmed civilians are not included in combat deaths, resulting in a discrepancy of two digits or more with literature estimates.

1988 Ntega and Mangara Crisis Uprising · 1988

In August 1988, riots broke out in the northern communes of Ntega and Mangara amid rumors that a local Tutsi strongman had provoked imminent massacres of Hutu farmers. Hundreds of Tutsi civilians died, and the military was subsequently deployed to quell the unrest with further bloodshed. This was followed by U.S. congressional hearings in September 1988 and a non-binding resolution calling for an impartial investigation, accountability, and refugee repatriation — described as one trigger for the constitutional and political reforms of the Buyoya government and the multiparty presidential and parliamentary elections of 1993 (Lemarchand).

1993 Assassination of President Ndadaye and Civil War Civil War · 1993–2005

In 1993, the first Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, was inaugurated following multiparty presidential and parliamentary elections; however, he was assassinated during a coup attempt on October 21, 1993. Amnesty International recorded that the Burundian armed forces were responsible for the coup attempt and assassination, as well as subsequent massacres and human rights violations investigated thereafter. The UN Security Council established an international commission of inquiry to investigate the facts surrounding the assassination and subsequent massacres and serious violence in August 28, 1995. Following this, a civil war ensued between government forces and rebel groups including CNDD-FDD and Palipehutu-FNL, with JusticeInfo (cited by AFP) recording 300,000 deaths from the 1993–2006 civil war.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
Civil War Deaths, 1993–2006No government tally in verified sources300,000 (JusticeInfo, cited by AFP)

Data Record: COW records this as two separate entries, 1993–1998 (combat deaths: 5,000) and 2001–2003 (3,150), while UCDP groups it under a single government conflict for the 1965–2024 period (ID 287, 4 years with over 1,000 war deaths). P&T records both July 3, 1993 and October 21, 1993 as 'failed' coups — the president was killed on October 21, but the coup forces did not seize power.

2015 Third-Term Protest, Coup Attempt, and Political Crisis Protest · 2015–2018

On April 25, 2015, the ruling CNDD-FDD nominated President Nkurunziza for a third term; the next day, on April 26, thousands gathered in the capital Bujumbura despite a ban on protests, and nearly daily protests continued for about six weeks, with several people killed or arrested by police crackdowns. The opposition argued that a third term violated the constitution and the peace agreement ending the civil war. A coup attempt led by the former chief of defense staff failed on May 13, and Nkurunziza won a third term in elections held amid tension on July 21. In October 2016, Burundi notified the International Criminal Court (ICC) of its withdrawal; the withdrawal took effect one year later, and the ICC opened a formal investigation into alleged crimes against humanity in November 2017. On May 17, 2018, a referendum on a constitutional amendment enabling rule until 2034 was scheduled.

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

1977 Coup by Supporters of René Coup · 1977

In 1977, while President James Mancham was attending the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in London, supporters of Prime Minister France-Albert René mobilized Tanzanian troops to stage an armed coup and René took the presidency (Daily Maverick). The same article notes that following the 1979 election, a socialist one-party state was established, with nationalizations of businesses, land expropriations, and the creation of a national youth corps, along with the abolition of free press and private schools. Records also exist indicating that René's side denied responsibility for the coup.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
FatalitiesNo government figures in verified sourcesNo figures in verified sources

Data Record: Powell & Thyne record 1977-06-05 as a 'successful' coup, but the Archigos 4.1 abnormal leader turnover table contains no entry for Seychelles (discrepancy between datasets).

  1. Daily Maverick, 'Seychelles: From putsches to development pushes' (2018-06-12) · Major media (South Africa) · Tone: Retrospective article from a South African perspective, critically describing the 1977–79 regime — https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2018-06-12-seychelles-from-putsches-to-development-pushes/

1981 Mike Hoare Mercenary Coup Attempt Coup · 1981

On November 25, 1981, around 5:30 PM, Major Mike Hoare and 43 mercenaries mainly from South Africa and Rhodesia landed at Seychelles International Airport on Mahé Island. Their goal was to seize the government for former President Mancham. The plan was revealed when airport security personnel found AK-47s in the mercenaries' luggage, leading to a shootout; the mercenaries then fled back to South Africa aboard an Air India passenger flight and were arrested and tried (Daily Maverick). In his 1982 trial, Hoare testified that the South African government knew of the plan, that the South African Defense Force provided weapons, and that the plan had been discussed since 1977. Prime Minister P. W. Botha stated immediately after the incident that the government neither initiated nor approved it (Christian Science Monitor). The accounts of the two parties conflict.

Number of Mercenaries43, including Hoare (Daily Maverick; 43 defendants in CSM trial)

  2. Christian Science Monitor, 'Mercenary trial highlights question of S. Africa link to Seychelles coup' (1982-05-05) · Major media (United States) · Tone: Report during the trial, centered on Hoare's testimony — https://www.csmonitor.com/1982/0505/050548.html

1982 Military Mutiny Uprising · 1982

In August 1982, soldiers mutinied over service conditions and seized a broadcasting station; however, they were suppressed by Tanzanian troops at President René's request (Daily Maverick). Subsequently, in 1991, René announced the return to a multiparty system; René won the elections of 1993, 1998, and 2001; and in the 2016 parliamentary election, the opposition Seychelles Democratic Alliance (LDS) won.

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

Dervish Movement (Muhammad Abdullah Hassan, 1899–1920) Uprising · 1899–1920

According to HistoryNet (Derek O'Connor, Aviation History, July 2012), the Dervish forces led by Muhammad Abdullah Hassan fought British Somaliland for approximately 20 years prior to World War I, and the British launched four major expeditions. In 1914, when many British troops withdrew, Hassan built stone fortifications. The British Royal Air Force 'Z Force' arrived in Berbera on December 30, 1919, and attacked the Medis and Jidali forts for the first time on January 21, 1920; it bombed Galbeybur on January 29 and the Talle (Taleh) fort early February. Hassan fled to Abyssinia (Ethiopia), where he died in November 1920 (presumed influenza). British records describe him as a 'mad mullah,' while accounts by his followers and Somali nationalists portray him as an anti-colonial religious leader. This narrative presents these differing accounts side by side without adjudicating between them.

October 1969 Military Coup of Siad Barre Coup · 1969

According to the Library of Congress Country Studies (Somalia: A Country Study), President Shermaarke was killed by his bodyguards on October 15, 1969 (the perpetrator was later tried and executed by the revolutionary government), and Prime Minister Igaal was abroad at the time. On October 21, military units seized strategic positions in Mogadishu, arrested government officials and prominent politicians, and received police cooperation. The new governing body, the Supreme Revolutionary Council (SRC), seated Major General Siad Barre as chairman; however, the Country Study does not characterize him as the mastermind of the coup. The SRC detained Igaal and other civilian leadership in the presidential palace. Modern data tables (Powell & Thyne · Archigos) record Barre's rule from 1969-10-21 to 1991-01-26, and also include the 1961-12-10 and 1978-04-09 coups (attempts).

Northern Civil War and Bombing of Hargeisa and Burao (1988–1991) Civil War · 1988–1991

According to Al Jazeera (James Reinl, 2014-02-06), from 1984 to 1988 the government forces arrested members of the Isaaq clans suspected of links with the Somali National Movement (SNM), and in 1988 the Barre government sent aircraft and troops to Hargeisa, an SNM stronghold, turning the city into ruins. The Somaliland Commission of Inquiry counted 226 mass graves, and the first remains were revealed by heavy rains in May 1997. In 2012, a U.S. court ruled that former Prime Minister of the Barre government, Mohammed Ali Samantar, must pay $21 million in damages. The Somaliland side described it as a massacre of Isaaq people, while the Barre government described it as suppression of rebels.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources

Data Record: COW records it as the 'First Somalia War of 1988-1991' (government vs. SNM, combat deaths 25,000), and UCDP records it as Conflict 337 (1982–). Civilian casualties of genocidal nature fall under a different category from combat fatalities.

  1. Al Jazeera — James Reinl, 'Investigating genocide in Somaliland' (2014-02-06) · Major news outlet · Orientation: Qatari state-funded media; centered on the Somaliland Commission of Inquiry and victim testimony — https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2014/2/6/investigating-genocide-in-somaliland

Collapse of the Barre Regime and State Disintegration & UN Intervention (1991–1995) Regime Overthrow · 1991–1995

According to the U.S. Department of State Office of the Historian, in January 1991 rebel forces drove Siad Barre out of Mogadishu. Al Jazeera (2014) reports that Somaliland declared secession approximately four months later. In April 1992, UNOSOM was established under UN Security Council Resolution 751, and in December 1992 the United States launched Operation Restore Hope with UN approval. UNITAF transitioned to UNOSOM II in March 1993. On October 3, 1993, forces under Mohamed Farah Aidid shot down two Black Hawk helicopters, resulting in the deaths of 18 U.S. soldiers and hundreds of Somalis in combat. The United States withdrew in March 1994, and the UN withdrew in March 1995, while fighting continued. The U.S. side described it as a humanitarian intervention, while Aidid's side described it as resistance against foreign military intervention.

Famine Deaths in 1991–92UnconfirmedNot verified on the source page (unverified)

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

October Revolution of 1964 — Abd al-Rahman's Military Regime Steps Down Protest · 1964

According to Willow Berridge (African Arguments, 2019-01-07), the 1964 uprising began with clashes between students and police at the University of Khartoum and spread into a broader movement; Ibrahim Abboud's military dictatorship agreed to step down after five days of protests. The movement was led by a coalition of trade unions in northern cities, and under pressure from junior and mid-ranking officers, the military intervened in favor of a transition to multi-party democracy. Islamists such as Hassan al-Turabi also participated alongside the Communist Party and the Umma Party. The Modern Data Table (Archigos) records Abd al-Rahman's tenure as 1958-11-18 to 1964-11-01. According to Berridge (2014-10-20), on October 21, 1964, students at the University of Khartoum clashed with police while discussing the political situation, and student activist Ahmad al-Kurayshi was killed by police gunfire, becoming the first casualty of the revolution. A general strike led by the Sudanese Medical Association, the Sudanese Bar Association, and the Khartoum University lecturers' union dissolved the 'November regime' two days after its declaration. After the revolution, two protesters were shot dead by the military in Al-Fashir.

April Intifada of 1985 — Fall of the Nimeiri Regime Protest · 1985

According to Berridge (2019), the 1985 uprising erupted after years of economic instability, triggered by an increase in basic commodity prices, and ended with the fall of Jaafar Nimeiri's 'May regime' after 11 days of protests. Nimeiri was ill at the time and had been in the United States when the uprising began. As in 1964, a coalition of political and professional unions led the movement, and the military intervened in favor of transition. Islamists turned their back on the government two weeks before the uprising but did not join the opposition intifada. The coup data table records 1985-04-06.

5. Modern Events through Literature

Eritrean War of Independence (1961–1991) Civil War · 1961–1991

According to a 2003 Human Rights Watch report, Emperor Haile Selassie unilaterally annexed Eritrea in 1962 and declared it an Ethiopian province, leading to decades of war for independence. Armed struggle began with the Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF) in 1961 (cited in a U.S. Congressional Research Service country analysis), and forces that broke away from the ELF in the mid-1960s renamed themselves the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) in 1977. By the early 1980s, the EPLF had become dominant among the liberation fronts, and the Derg government rejected its proposal for an internationally supervised referendum on independence. In May 1991, shortly after the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) seized Addis Ababa, the EPLF took Asmara. In a UN-supervised referendum held April 23–25, 1993, 99.80% of 1,168,978 participants voted for independence; the Ethiopian government and the UN certified the vote as 'free and fair.' The Ethiopian government's account records the annexation as a decision of the federal parliament, while the liberation front accounts describe it as an imposed annexation. This narrative presents the different accounts side by side without adjudicating between them.

Ethiopia–Eritrea Border War (1998–2000) Civil War · 1998–2000

Although an interstate war, this event had a decisive impact on subsequent domestic governance structures and is therefore recorded together. According to Human Rights Watch (2003), clashes in the Badme area in May–June 1998 escalated into full-scale war by early June, and fighting at the Battle of Lotame in early 1999 alone resulted in 'thousands' of casualties on both sides. An agreement to cease hostilities was signed at the Algiers OAU-mediated talks on June 18, 2000, followed by a comprehensive peace agreement on December 12, 2000. HRW (2009) records that large-scale conscription resumed and demobilization halted during the war. Both governments blame each other for starting the war.

G-15 Open Letter and Arrests/Shutdown of Independent Media in September 2001 Protest · 2001

According to Human Rights Watch (2009), in May 2001, 15 of 75 Central Committee members of the ruling People's Democratic and Just Party (PFDJ) issued an open letter criticizing the president. The government arrested 11 of the G-15 on September 18, 2001, and on September 19 it revoked the licenses of eight independent newspapers and arrested ten journalists. The government stated that the newspapers had violated the 1996 Press Proclamation and undermined national unity. As of March 2009, the 11 G-15 members and journalists were cut off from external contact without having been charged or tried; HRW estimated that 5,000–10,000 people, excluding deserters, were detained without charge. Although this was an expression of public dissent within the ruling party rather than street protests, it is classified under the closest category in the Country Analysis Series's 'protest' classification.

Forto Incident — Information Ministry Occupation (2013-01-21) Coup · 2013

According to Reporters Without Borders (RSF, 2013-01-24), on January 21, 2013, approximately 100 soldiers occupied the Information Ministry building ('Forto') atop Asmara Hill. Reports indicated that four commanders led the occupation, including Colonel Saleh Osman. The soldiers had the Eri-TV director, Asmelash Abreha, read two statements: one demanded the implementation of the 1997 Constitution, whose enforcement had been suspended after the 1998–2000 war, and the other called for the release of political prisoners and those arrested for attempting to leave the country illegally. After the two statements were read, broadcasting was cut off and replaced with recorded footage. Tanks surrounded the building, and state broadcasting was interrupted for approximately 12 hours before resuming around 10 PM. The soldiers withdrew in the evening, and no reports of gunfire or arrests emerged. The government remained silent initially; the following day, President's advisor Yemane Ghebreab stated that the situation was calm and redirected foreign media reports to 'enemies of Eritrea.' Foreign media access was restricted, making detailed verification difficult.

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

December 1960 Royal Bodyguard Coup Attempt Coup · 1960

According to the U.S. Library of Congress Country Study (Ethiopia: A Country Study), on December 13, 1960, while Emperor Haile Selassie was abroad, Commander Mengistu Neway of the Royal Bodyguard, his followers, some security officials including Police Commissioner, and radical intellectuals including his younger brother Girma Melese Neway staged a coup. The coup forces initially succeeded by capturing more than 20 people in Addis Ababa, including the Crown Prince and ministers, but failed to gain popular support as the army and air force remained loyal to the emperor and the head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church supported the loyalists. The emperor returned to the capital on December 17. The Country Study describes that although the attempt failed, it weakened the claim that monarchy was universally accepted and polarized traditional and modern forces.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
DeathsUnconfirmedNo figures in the annual page (Country Study) (unverified)
High-ranking officials taken hostageUnconfirmedMore than 20 people including the Crown Prince and ministers (U.S. Library of Congress Country Study)

Data record: In the UCDP Government Conflict List, 'Military faction (forces of Mengistu Neway)' corresponds to this event. The record in the coup data set follows this national data table.

  1. U.S. Library of Congress, Ethiopia: A Country Study — 'The Attempted Coup of 1960 and Its Aftermath' (reprinted on countrystudies.us) · Government-published country study · Orientation: U.S. government publication (written during the Cold War), academic editing — https://countrystudies.us/ethiopia/23.htm

1974 Revolution — Military Mutiny, Strikes, Protests, and Abdication of the Emperor Regime Overthrow · 1974

According to the U.S. Library of Congress Country Study, on January 12, 1974, in Negelle, Sidamo Province, the 4th Infantry Brigade mutinied over food and water conditions, and discontent spread to other units including the 2nd Division in Asmara, Eritrea. In February, protests peaked over fuel prices, educational reforms, and low teacher salaries; Prime Minister Aklilu Habte Wold resigned, and Endalkachew Mekonnen succeeded him on February 28. By late June, about 120 officers below the rank of major formed the 'Derg' and elected Mengistu Haile Mariam as chairman. On September 12, the Derg officially deposed and imprisoned Emperor Haile Selassie, and changed its name to the Provisional Military Administrative Council (PMAC) three days later. The royal account records this as a military mutiny, while the revolutionary account records it as a revolution following popular uprising. This narrative presents both accounts side by side without adjudicating.

Data record: Archigos is likely to record Haile Selassie's departure in 1974 as an irregular exit; the exact code will follow this national data table. Because the MM dataset covers only from 1990 onward, the 1974 protests and strikes are not included.

Collapse of the Derg Regime and Capture of the Capital by EPRDF and EPLF (1991) Regime Overthrow · 1991

According to Human Rights Watch (2003), the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) captured Asmara in May 1991, shortly after the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) seized Addis Ababa. With this, the Derg regime that had ruled since 1974 came to an end, and Eritrea achieved separation and independence in April 1993 through a UN-supervised referendum. COW records this period as the 'Tigrean & Eritrean War of 1982-1991' (opponents TPLF and EPLF).

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

Amin's 1971 Coup and the 1979 Regime Collapse Coup · 1971–1979

The Powell & Thyne coup data records the January 25, 1971 coup as 'successful', while Archigos records Obote's ouster as 'removed by a military without foreign support' and Amin's ouster (1979-04-11) as 'removed under threat of foreign military force' (see data table). UCDP records the Tanzania–Uganda interstate conflict (ID 427, territorial) separately. Estimates of deaths during the Amin era vary widely across sources, and no figures were found on the original pages consulted for this round, so they remain unverified. The government at the time denied reports of large-scale killings.

Data record: P&T coup 1971-01-25 (successful). Coup attempts on 1974-03-23 and 1974-11-11 are also listed in the data table. The 1979 regime collapse is recorded as resulting from an interstate war (UCDP 427) rather than a coup.

The Bush War (NRA armed struggle, 1981–1986) Civil War · 1981–1986

The Christian Science Monitor (1984-09-20) reported that the second Obote government was unable to suppress the guerrilla war led by Museveni's National Resistance Army (NRA). The same article stated that Museveni estimated that '300,000 people have died across Uganda since 1981', Paul Ssemogerere of the opposition Democratic Party viewed 500,000 as a more accurate figure since 1980, and U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Human Rights Elliott Abrams testified before Congress in August 1984 that more than 100,000 had died in recent years. The article does not include an official government death toll. On July 27, 1985, Obote was ousted in a military coup and the Okello government took power; Archigos records that Okello was 'removed by rebels without foreign support' on January 29, 1986. It is noted alongside that the highest estimates came from parties to the conflict.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Deaths, 1980/81–1984No official figure from the Obote government (CSM 1984)NRA Museveni 300,000 (since 1981), Democratic Party Ssemogerere 500,000 (since 1980), U.S. State Dept. Abrams over 100,000 (cited by CSM 1984)

Data record: While the COW civil war list does not separately record this war, it appears in UCDP 314 (government vs. NRA, etc.), NAVCO 'National Resistance Army' (1980–1986), and P&T's 1985-07-27 coup. The discrepancy across datasets is recorded as an anomaly.

The LRA Conflict and the International Criminal Court Case Civil War · 1986–2006

NAVCO records LRA's armed campaign against the Museveni government from 1986 to 2017. According to the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Ugandan government referred the matter to the ICC, and arrest warrants for five LRA leaders including Joseph Kony were issued on July 8, 2005 in camera and released on October 13. The amended indictment of April 17, 2025 holds that Kony committed at least 39 war crimes and crimes against humanity in northern Uganda from July 1, 2002 to December 31, 2005. On November 6, 2025, the pre-trial chamber confirmed all 39 charges, but a trial cannot be held under the Rome Statute without the accused present, so Kony remains at large. The LRA cited the treatment of northern residents by government forces as the reason for resistance, while the government characterized the LRA as a terrorist organization. This narrative presents both sides' accounts side by side without adjudicating them.

September 2009 Kampala Riots (Blocking King Kyungu's Visit to Kyanguli) Protest · 2009

According to Human Rights Watch (2010-09-10), rioting broke out in Kampala for two days when police blocked a visit by the Buganda Kingdom delegation to Kyanguli on September 10, 2009. Kabaka (King of Buganda) planned the visit to coincide with National Youth Day, but leaders of the Banyala who do not recognize Kabaka's authority opposed it. Supporters of Kabaka took to the streets. The government reported 27 deaths, most from 'grenades' fired by security personnel, while HRW and other investigations estimated over 40 based on hospital records. At least 31 people were charged with terrorism for arson of vehicles and police stations; two security personnel (one Special Police officer, one soldier) were charged with murder but no trial was held, and the parliamentary inquiry committee did not call a single witness.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

1935 Copperbelt Black Miners Strike Protest · 1935

According to the Swarthmore College Global Nonviolent Action Database (GNAD), black miners at the Roan & Antelope (Luanwashi), Mupfure, and Nkana mines in the Copperbelt of Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia) went on strike from May 20 to 29, 1935, protesting colonial authorities' tax increases. In the Roan & Antelope mine, askaris (local recruits in the colonial forces) beat striking miners with clubs and then opened fire, killing six and wounding 22. The commission of inquiry established by the colonial authorities found that the tax increase was 'fair and reasonable' and that there was no basis for the strike, but it acknowledged corporal punishment at Mupfure as one cause, created some oversight committees, and dismissed a poorly regarded district officer. The same database notes both views: that the outcome was 'formal change' and that it influenced colonial policy. Left-wing journalist George Padmore claimed 29 deaths and 73 injuries, but this figure does not match other sources and is left unverified.

1964 Runda Church Uprising (Runda Conflict) Uprising · 1964

Clashes between followers of the separatist church 'Lumpa', led by Alice Lenshina, and supporters of the soon-to-take-power United National Independence Party (UNIP) escalated into armed conflict in 1964. According to Wim van Binsbergen's research page at the African Studies Centre, Leiden University, the Governor of Northern Rhodesia declared a state of emergency in July 1964; fighting between government forces and Lumpa adherents in northeastern rural areas ended in October 1964, with approximately 1,500 deaths estimated. Other accounts cite around 700. The Lumpa side rejected the authority of the secular government and taxation, operated its own courts, and viewed these as a threat to order. Historiography has debated whether to characterize this event as a 'rebellion' or a 'massacre' (Gordon 2008). This article does not adjudicate but presents both accounts side by side.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources

Because it is an event from the colonial period immediately preceding independence (1964-10-24), there is a possibility that it falls outside the scope of capture for country-level datasets.

June 1990 Cornmeal Price Riots and Luchembe Coup Attempt Coup · 1990

According to UPI (1990-06-26), the price of cornmeal, a staple that month, had risen by 100%, prompting students at the University of Zambia to begin protesting President Kaunda's delay in multiparty democracy and his inability to feed the nation; the protests spread into Lusaka city center, where dozens of shops were looted. The same report stated that at least 25 people died and approximately 80 were injured, with hospital sources indicating that most victims were under 20 years old and included police officers. Authorities reported over 100 arrests. The article also mentions the Copperbelt riots of December 1986. On June 30, 1990 (Powell & Thyne date), Lieutenant Mwamba Luchembe announced on state radio that the military had seized power, but the attempt failed within hours. UPI (1990-08-01) reported that Kaunda pardoned Luchembe and other coup plotters and ordered the release of students detained in the riots. NAVCO records the 1990–1991 anti-one-party rule nonviolent campaign as 'successful'.

October 28, 1997 Coup Attempt Coup · 1997

The Powell & Thyne coup data records the October 28, 1997 coup attempt as a 'failure' (see data table). Part of the military seized state broadcasters to announce the seizure of the Chiluba government, but government forces recaptured the facilities; a state of emergency was subsequently declared, and many people, including former President Kaunda, were detained. Original texts from the U.S. Department of State and Amnesty International regarding detention numbers, allegations of torture, and casualties could not be accessed in this round and are therefore not included. The government prosecuted it as a treason case, while the detained opposition argued that it was political repression.

5. Modern Events through the Literature

FRUD Armed Uprising (Djiboutian Civil War, 1991–2001) Civil War · 1991–2001

According to the University of Edinburgh PA-X Peace Agreement Database, an internal war began in 1991 between the ruling Rassemblement Populaire pour le Progrès (RPP) government and the Front for the Restoration of Unity and Democracy (FRUD), whose main faction was Awar. The same source's background narrative states that while the Awar constituted a significant share of the population, they felt marginalized by their exclusion from government. When Awar forces seized northern army outposts, French troops moved north to support the government. Negotiations in November 1992 and May 1993 failed; a peace agreement was signed between the government and some FRUD factions on December 26, 1994, combat declined with the transition to multiparty politics, but radical factions continued small-scale armed resistance until they signed an agreement in 2001. The FRUD side cited exclusion of the Awar as the reason for the uprising, while the government side emphasized suppressing armed rebellion and national reunification. The total death toll could not be verified from the source text consulted in this round.

Anti-government protest on February 18, 2011 Protest · 2011

Following a constitutional amendment in 2010 that removed the presidential term limit, protests opposing President Guelleh's bid for a third term were held on February 18, 2011. According to Human Rights Watch (HRW, 2011-04-04), security forces violently dispersed the protest and arrested dozens of protesters and bystanders, detaining three opposition leaders for one day. Over 100 people were charged with assault and unauthorized protests; on February 27, when approximately 80 appeared in court, a judge dismissed 40 cases, prompting the minister of justice to replace him, and the new judge sentenced 25 to prison terms. On March 3, the minister of interior refused permission for protests citing the violence of February 18, after which protests were banned outright. The government cited the February 18 violence as justification for the ban, while HRW viewed it as a violation of Article 15 of the constitution and the ICCPR. The HRW document does not report a death toll.

Outbreak on December 21, 2015 (Buldhuqo shooting) Protest · 2015

According to a joint statement by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the Djiboutian League for Human Rights (LDDH) (2015-12-23), clashes broke out at a religious ceremony site in the Buldhuqo area of Boudhle outside Djibouti City on the morning of December 21, killing two people; military forces including presidential guards then opened fire with live ammunition, resulting in at least 25 more deaths and over 27 dead and over 150 injured. Clashes also occurred later that afternoon at a meeting place of seven opposition coalition (USN) leaders. The government spokesperson, Foreign Minister Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, announced 7 deaths (including one girl) and 50 police injuries, while Interior Minister Hassan Omar stated that the ceremony had been organized by 'malicious individuals instructed by foreign sponsors.' Both accounts are presented side by side without adjudication.

2. Before the Industrial Revolution (~1759) — Records of Uprisings and Peasant Wars

1631 Mombasa Uprising (Seizure of Fort Jesus) Portuguese Era Swahili Coast · 1631–1632

According to the Dictionary of African Christian Biography (DACB), written by Aylward Shorter, Yusuf al-Hassan, who grew up in the Augustinian order and was baptized as 'Jerome' and became a Portuguese-protected sultan in 1626, entered Fort Jesus on August 16, 1631, killed the Portuguese commander, and the uprising began. The same entry records those who died for refusing conversion as '288 men, women, and children' and divides them into 47 Portuguese men, 39 women, and 59 children and 72 African men and their families. The sultan left Mombasa in 1632, Portuguese rule returned, and the Goa Bishop's Council collected witness testimonies in 1632–1633. The Portuguese and church sides describe this as martyrdom, while the sultan's tradition describes it as resistance to foreign rule. Dates (15th/16th) and casualty figures differ across sources.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

Mau Mau Uprising and State of Emergency (1952–1960) Uprising · 1952–1960

According to Bernard Porter's review of David Anderson's Histories of the Hanged and Caroline Elkins's The Burden of Empire in the London Review of Books (2005), the colonial government's official figure for combat deaths among Mau Mau was approximately 12,000, while Anderson estimated that actual combat deaths 'would have exceeded 20,000.' Britain hanged 1,090 Kikuyu people and 32 white settlers died. Regarding Elkins's estimate, a reader letter in the same publication disputed the claim of up to 100,000 interned as inaccurate, while Elkins had argued that up to 300,000 Kikuyu died during the state of emergency. The colonial government described it as counter-terrorism, whereas Mau Mau and later scholarship describe it as a struggle for land and freedom. Both accounts are presented without adjudication.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Combat Deaths Mau MauApprox. 12,000 (colonial government official figure, cited by LRB)Over 20,000 (Anderson 2005)
Executions1,090—
Total Kikuyu Deaths During State of Emergency—Up to 300,000 (Elkins, cited in LRB letter — disputed)

Data Record: UCDP 241 (government vs. Mau Mau) · NAVCO 'Mau Mau Rebellion' are listed in this data table. Official figures are cited differently across sources as 11,000, 11,503, and 12,000.

London Review of Books 27(5), 2005 · Academic book review (major outlet) · Orientation: imperial history scholar's review, including a critical letter regarding Elkins' figures — https://www.lrb.co.uk/v27/n05/bernard-porter/how-did-they-get-away-with-it

August 1, 1982 Air Force Coup Attempt Coup · 1982

The Powell & Thyne coup data records the August 1, 1982 coup attempt as 'failed,' while UCDP 348 records government vs. a 'Hezekiah Ochuka faction' as an armed conflict (see data table). Official and independent casualty figures could not be verified in the sources consulted for this round.

Data Record: P&T 1982-08-01 (failed) · UCDP 348 capture this event. The NAVCO 'anti-Arap Moi' campaign is also listed in the data table.

  1. Powell & Thyne, Global Instances of Coups (data table) · Academic dataset · Orientation: neutral event coding — https://www.uky.edu/~clthyn2/coup_data/home.htm

Post-Election Violence in 2007–2008 Protest · 2007–2008

According to the Kenya section of Human Rights Watch's World Report 2009, the post-election violence commission established by the government (CIPEV, also known as the Waki Commission) stated that 'at least 1,133 people were killed and more than 300,000 displaced.' Police used live ammunition in early unrest, killing over 400, and the commission noted excessive use of force by police. In November 2008, the UN estimated that 113,761 people remained in camps, but the government counted far fewer at 3,170 households. A report in October 2008 found that senior politicians from both major parties organized and incited violence and recommended the establishment of a special tribunal; if not implemented, it suggested transferring a list of those implicated to the International Criminal Court. Each party blamed the other for responsibility.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

Overthrow of the Abdallah Government Immediately After Independence in 1975 Coup · 1975

Comoros gained independence from France on July 6, 1975 (Al Jazeera country overview). The same overview notes that a coup began just weeks after independence, and that the first president, Ahmed Abdallah, was ousted by French mercenaries led by Captain Bob Denard. Subsequently, the island nation has experienced more than 20 coups and coup attempts, according to the same source.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Number of Coups and Attempts Since Independence (as of 2004)No government tally in verified dataMore than 20 times (Al Jazeera 2004)

Data Record: Powell & Thyne records 1975-08-03 as a 'successful' coup, while Archigos 4.1 records Abdallah's departure as 'Removed by Rebels, without Foreign Support'. The Al Jazeera overview notes French mercenaries' involvement, conflicting with the coding of foreign support.

  1. Al Jazeera, 'Comoros: Country profile' (2004-09-01) · Major media (Qatar) · Orientation: Brief overview, emphasizing France's role — https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2004/9/1/comoros-country-profile

Mercenary Interventions in 1978 and 1989 and Abdallah's Return and Death Coup · 1978–1989

The Al Jazeera overview notes that France used mercenaries four times to effect regime change after independence, and that Denard appeared in several subsequent power struggles. Details of Abdallah's return to power in 1978 following Denard's intervention and his death in November 1989 in an incident related to the presidential guard could not be verified from the sources consulted for this round (see unverified items). The data records are as follows.

  1. Al Jazeera, 'Comoros: Country profile' (2004-09-01) · Major media (Qatar) · Orientation: Brief overview — https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2004/9/1/comoros-country-profile

Separation Declarations by Anjouan and Mohéli in 1997 and Armed Conflict Civil War · 1997–2002

Violent clashes broke out when the islands of Anjouan and Mohéli declared independence from Comoros in 1997 (Al Jazeera). It was not until 2002 that the central government granted autonomy to the three islands, including Grande Comore; each island elected its own president and drafted a constitution, while the central government retained security and fiscal authority, according to the same source. The African Union and Francophone organizations encouraged negotiations between the central government and the island authorities.

Bloodless Coup by Colonel Azali in 1999 Coup · 1999

Colonel Azali Assoumani took power in a bloodless coup in 1999, and the central government led by him retained control of security and finance even after the 2002 autonomy arrangement (Al Jazeera 2004).

Operation to Land on Anjouan in 2008 Civil War · 2008

In an operation announced by President Ahmed Abdallah Sambi, Comoros government forces and Tanzanian and Sudanese African Union troops (totaling about 1,400) landed on Anjouan in the early morning, with logistical support from Libya, France, and the United States (VOA). The coalition encountered some resistance near the residence of Colonel Mohamed Bacar in Baraka. Bacar, a former policeman trained in France, had been elected president of Anjouan under the new constitution but was re-elected in 'last year' in an internationally unrecognized election; the government sought to arrest and try him on charges of insubordination, corruption, and human rights violations. The African Union viewed Bacar's proposal for new elections as a delaying tactic. VOA notes that Comoros has experienced 'several secession attempts' and more than ten coups or attempted coups led by foreign mercenaries over its 32 years of independence.

5. Modern Events in the Literature

1964 Zanzibar Revolution Overthrow of the Regime · 1964

On Sunday, January 12, 1964, the newly elected Zanzibari government collapsed. Over the next week, the sultan left the island, thousands lost their lives, and most of the victims were Omani Arabs (Leiden African Studies Centre). Several months later, Zanzibar united with mainland Tanganyika to form Tanzania. The same source notes that memories of this event have split in two: many Afro-Zanzibaris commemorate it as the beginning of true independence from colonial and Arab feudal rule, while others mourn it as a massacre. An Omani author, Aliyami, characterizes the revolution as an 'invasion' by mainland forces, emphasizing colonial policies and the responsibility of Nyerere and Kamuzu; a reviewer notes that this book has a pro-Arab bias and downplays the role of Arab plantation owners (citing Cooper's research showing that many clove plantations were owned by Arabs). Accounts from both parties are presented side by side.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
DeathsNo government tally in confirmed sources4,000–20,000 (range across multiple sources; Leiden ASC 2014)

Data record: Archigos 4.1 records the departure of Prime Minister Shamte Hamadi (1964-01-12) as 'Removed by Rebels, without Foreign Support' and the irregular accession of Karume. UCDP/PRIO and Powell & Thyne have no records (in 1964, Zanzibar was a separate state immediately after independence, and whether its country code is linked to Tanzania may vary across datasets).

C. van de Bruinhorst (2014-01) · Academic institution review · Tone: Introduces the pro-Arab narrative of an Omani author while appending a critical assessment — https://www.ascleiden.nl/content/library-highlights/zanzibar-personalities-events-1828-1972

January 2001 Zanzibar and Pemba Protests Shooting Protest · 2001

Human Rights Watch notes that there was widespread electoral fraud in Zanzibar in the October 2000 national elections. About three months later, on January 27, 2001, security forces fired on supporters of the Civic United Front (CUF) protesting electoral fraud, and abuses continued into late January. The main sites were Zanzibar Town and the Pemba towns of Wete, Micheweni, and Chake-Chake. Government and CUF/HRW casualty tallies differ substantially; HRW states that it cannot determine the exact number and that its figures are approximations starting from government and media figures. HRW also notes that the 1995 and 2000 elections were poorly conducted, leading most donor countries to suspend aid to the Zanzibari government.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The 1948 Christianborg Crossroads Shooting and the Accra Riots Protest · 1948

According to the Ghana News Agency (GNA, state-run news agency), on February 28, 1948, World War II veterans marching to the Christiansborg Castle to deliver a petition regarding pensions and conditions of service were fired upon by police at an intersection, killing three leaders: Corporal Azito Atta, Lance-Corporal Attipoe, and Private Odartey Lamptey. Riots followed for five days in Accra and other cities, with Asian and European shops looted and additional deaths occurring. On the same day, the 'Big Six' led the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC) to send a telegram to the Colonial Secretary in London. The colonial government appointed the Watson Commission to investigate the causes, which subsequently led to constitutional reforms. Accounts of the order to fire and the shooters differ across sources; this article does not adjudicate.

Deaths from Crossroads ShootingColonial authorities' official total unverified in original text3 veterans (GNA 2026-02)

Data Record: Because this is an event from the colonial period (prior to 1957 independence), it falls outside the coverage of national-level datasets (COW, UCDP, MM). NAVCO records the CPP's independence movement as nonviolent and successful.

The 1966–1981 Coup Chain Coups · 1966–1981

The Powell & Thyne coup data records five successful coups (overthrow of the Nkrumah government on 1966-02-24, overthrow of the Busia government on 1972-01-13, ouster of Acheampong on 1978-07-05, AFRC seizure of power on 1979-06-04, and overthrow of the Limann government on 1981-12-31) and five failed coups (in 1967, 1979-05, 1982, 1983, and 1984). Archigos records Nkrumah's and Busia's exiles, Akufo's death, and Acheampong's and Limann's imprisonments as outcomes of irregular exits. UCDP codes the period 1966–1983 as armed conflict between government and military factions (active in three years, no year with over 1,000 war deaths). Casualties for individual coups could not be verified from official or independent sources in this round.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Number of Coups (1966–1984)—5 successes, 5 failures (Powell & Thyne)

Data Record: P&T records the 1979-06-04 event as a successful coup, but Archigos records the start of Rawlings's first rule on 1979-06-05, a one-day difference. The 1978-07-05 ouster of Acheampong is classified in Archigos as 'an internal military power struggle that did not lead to a coup,' which differs from the definition used by P&T (successful coup).

  1. Powell & Thyne, Global Instances of Coups · Academic dataset · Orientation: Neutral event coding — https://www.uky.edu/~clthyn2/coup_data/home.htm

Failure of the May 15, 1979 uprising and the June 4 uprising; AFRC executions Coups · 1979

According to a guest column by retired Brigadier Dan Frimpong in the state daily Daily Graphic, the mutiny led by Air Force Lieutenant Jerry Rawlings on May 15, 1979 was suppressed by the reconnaissance battalion and Rawlings was put on trial for treason. On June 4, soldiers led by Corporal Tashiri of the 5th Infantry Battalion in Accra mutinied, freed Rawlings, and took him to the broadcasting station; the SMC2 government of General Akufo collapsed, and Rawlings became chairman of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC). In the process, Army Commander Oduartei-Wellington was killed resisting at Nima Police Station. On June 16, the AFRC executed Generals Achampong and Utuka; on June 26, it executed Akufo, Afrifa, Amadu-Me, Boakye, Kotey, and Pellie. The AFRC described this as 'house cleaning' against corruption, while critics including the author challenge the trial procedures. This article makes no judgment.

Northern Region Conflict of 1994 (Kokomba-Nanumba 'Cockfight War') Civil War · 1994–1996

According to the University of Edinburgh Peace Agreements Database (PA-X), a conflict broke out in northern Ghana between 1994 and 1996 among the Dagomba, Nanumba, Gonja, and minority ethnic group Kokomba. Known as the 'Cockfight War' after a dispute over horned chicken trading in villages, research views it primarily through land rights and chieftaincy (traditional political representation) issues. Military stabilization attempts failed, and an NGO-led peace process led to the Kumasi Peace Accord, addressing chieftaincy institutions, traditional systems, land rights, and reconciliation procedures. Deaths are estimated by the database at 2,000–15,000, while other studies and refugee agency data suggest figures in the 1,000s to 2,000s, showing significant discrepancies.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The 1981 Coup Attempt by Kukoi Samba Sanneh and Senegalese Intervention Coup · 1981

According to an article in The Point (Gambia, 2021-07-30) citing historian Houssein Seydi, on July 30, 1981, civilian Kukoi Samba Sanneh, along with 11 others, began the uprising by raiding the Field Force armory in Bakau and made their first radio broadcast on Radio Gambia. President Jawara was in London for the wedding of the British heir apparent and invoked the 1965 defense pact with Senegal. Senegalese troops arrived in Banjul on August 1, suppressed the rebels, and the crisis lasted eight days. Kukoi fled to Bissau. The rebels took the president's family hostage, including his wife, but British special forces rescued them. Seydi says that approximately 1,000 Gambians died, and property worth about $5 million was looted or burned; several dozen Senegalese soldiers were killed, and all 18 on a Senegalese military helicopter shot down by rebels perished. More than 2,000 people were detained, many, including opposition leader S.M. Diab, were released, and no executions followed the treason trials.

The 1994 Coup by Lieutenant Jammeh Coup · 1994

The Powell & Thyne coup data records a successful coup on July 23, 1994 and an unsuccessful one on November 11 of the same year. Archigos notes that President Jawara was ousted by foreign-assistance-free troops on July 22, 1994 and went into exile, while Yahya Jammeh took power irregularly on the same day. Individual casualty and detainee figures could not be verified from the original sources in this round.

Bloody suppression of April 2000 student protests Protest · 2000

An Amnesty International emergency report (2000-04-11) recorded that security forces dispersed a protest organized by students on April 10–11 with 'excessive and indiscriminate force,' leaving 14 dead and at least 28 injured. The protests took place after authorities refused to grant permission for a rally by the Gambia Students' Union (GAMSU). According to JusticeInfo (2019), the triggers were suspicions that student Ebou Barry had died from blows by firefighters and an alleged sexual assault of a 15-year-old female track athlete, Vinta Mane. The vice president claimed that protesters were armed with guns, while officials blamed 'delinquents, not students.' A nine-member investigative committee heard 59 testimonies and in its August 2000 report rejected government claims, recommending prosecution of security personnel who had opened fire while also recommending prosecution of seven student leaders who had led the protests. In April 2001, the National Assembly passed a law granting immunity to those involved in the crackdown, and no charges were brought over the deaths. The Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC) heard testimony from victims in 2019.

April 2016 election reform protests and death in custody of Solo Sandeng Protest · 2016

A joint statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and Article 19 (2016-04-18) reported that on April 14, a small protest demanding electoral reforms ahead of the December presidential election took place in Serrekunda, outside Banjul; security forces dispersed it and arrested many. Solo Sandeng, an executive member of the opposition United Democratic Party (UDP), was detained that day and died; the statement described his death as 'suspect.' The UDP claimed he had been killed under torture by the National Intelligence Agency (NIA) and that two other party members also died in custody. The youth leader Patutama Jallow was also reported to have suffered serious injuries while in detention. On April 16, a protest demanding an investigation into Sandeng's death and his release resulted in police firing tear gas and arresting at least five officials, including UDP representative Ousainou Darboe, and protesters. The government position is not included in the statement.

5. Modern Events as Recorded in the Literature

The 1984–2021 Coup Chain Coups · 1984–2021

The Powell & Thyne coup data records three successful coups (1984-04-03, overthrow of the Beavogui transitional government following Sekou Touré's death; 2008-12-23, takeover by Dadis Camara following Conte's death; 2021-09-05, overthrow of the Conde government) and three failed coups (1985, 1996, 2011). Archigos notes that Conte left office on 2008-12-22 by natural death and that Dadis Camara was removed from power by the military on 2009-12-05 and went into exile. Casualties for individual events could not be verified from official or independent sources in this round.

General Strike and Crackdown in January–February 2007 Protest · 2007

According to Human Rights Watch (2007-04-24), Guinea's major trade unions launched a nationwide general strike in mid-January 2007 protesting corruption, governance failures, and economic hardship (the third in less than a year). On January 22, security forces opened fire on unarmed protesters marching toward the National Assembly in Conakry; riots broke out when President Condé appointed Étienne Kourouma as prime minister in early February, leading to a state of emergency. The organization recorded that under martial law, the military searched homes under the pretext of searching for weapons and committed killings, rapes, and looting. In late February, Condé appointed Lansana Kouyaté as consensus prime minister, and a new government took office in late March pursuant to an agreement ending the strike. Based on interviews with 115 victims and witnesses, the organization tallied at least 129 deaths and over 1,700 injuries during the six-week crisis.

Massacre at the Conakry Stadium on September 28, 2009 Protest · 2009

According to UN News (2022-09-28), an opposition rally protesting the junta took place at the 'Stade du 28 Septembre' in Conakry on September 28, 2009; security forces blocked the stadium exits and then attacked. The UN International Commission of Inquiry confirmed 156 identified deaths and disappearances and at least 109 women and girls subjected to sexual violence and sexual abuse in its final report of December 2009; the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights stated that many had been tortured to death and buried in mass graves. A trial opened in Conakry on September 28, 2022, with 11 defendants, including former junta leader Moussa Dadis Camara. The junta's casualty figures at the time could not be verified from original sources in this round.

5. Modern Events through the Literature

1959 Finguiati Dock Strike Massacre Protest · 1959

According to an article by Priscilla Marques Campos published in Africa Is a Country (2023-12-08), on August 3, 1959, police, military, and armed Portuguese civilians suppressed striking dock workers at the Finguiati docks in Bissau Harbor who were demanding wages and working conditions, resulting in approximately 50 deaths and 100 injuries. Some police reportedly opposed the attack. Nationalist leaders had hoped that the strike would bring Portugal to the negotiating table, but their line radicalized after the violent suppression, and the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC) has remembered this event as a political catalyst for its armed struggle from 1963 to 1974. August 3 is currently a national holiday.

The PAIGC campaign in NAVCO 1.3 (1963–1974) is coded from the year armed struggle began.

1963–1974 PAIGC War of Independence Uprising · 1963–1974

UCDP/PRIO armed conflict data classifies the Portuguese government's territorial dispute with PAIGC as 'colonial-type (extrasystemic)', recording it as 11 active years from 1963 to 1973, and does not code years with more than 1,000 war deaths. NAVCO 1.3 records the same PAIGC campaign as a violence campaign against Portuguese occupation from 1963 to 1974. Independence was recognized following the 1974 Portuguese Carnation Revolution, and Archigos records that Luis Cabral took power via an irregular route on September 10, 1974.

1998–1999 Mane Military Junta Civil War Civil War · 1998–1999

Powell & Thyne records June 7, 1998, as a failed coup and May 7, 1999, as a successful coup. COW Civil War v5.1 classifies the '1998–1999 Guinea-Bissau military war' as an internationalized civil war between the government and the Mane Military Junta, coding 2,000 combat deaths and a result code of 2. UCDP records 1998–1999 as two years of an internationalized civil-war-type government conflict against the 'Military Junta for Consolidation of Democracy, Peace, and Justice' but does not code it as a year with more than 1,000 war deaths. Senegalese and Guinean forces intervened on the government side. Archigos notes that Vieira was ousted by the military on May 7, 1999, and went into exile, while Ansumane Mane held power from May 7 to May 14, 1999. The scale of displacement could not be verified from original sources in this round.

2009 Assassinations of President Vieira and Chief of Staff Tagmé Nawaï Regime Overthrow · 2009

According to Al Jazeera (2009-03-03), Chief of Defense Staff Batista Tagmé Nawaï was killed by a bomb placed under the stairs of his office, and several hours later President Vieira was shot dead by soldiers as he attempted to leave his residence. The forensic pathologist stated that the president had been severely beaten before being shot multiple times in the neck and face. Subsequently, the speaker of parliament took office as acting head of state in accordance with the constitution.

  1. Al Jazeera, 'Guinea-Bissau gets interim leader' (2009-03-03) · Major outlet (international broadcaster) · Orientation: Reporting immediately after the event, citing official and medical sources — https://www.aljazeera.com/news/africa/2009/03/200933144618292875.html

Military Coup Just Before the November 2025 Election Coup · 2025

According to the International IDEA Democracy Tracker (November 2025 issue), military officers seized power on November 26, one day before the announcement of the presidential election results on November 23. President Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias were both claiming victory at the time, and General Orta Etam took office as transitional president for a 'one-year period.' The National Electoral Commission stated on December 2 that tally sheets and most of the computerized system had been destroyed, preventing the release of final results. Opposition figures were arrested, and six were released on December 23, but opposition leader Domingos Simões Pereira remained detained. Some opposition and regional actors questioned whether the coup had been staged to halt the vote count. ECOWAS and the African Union suspended Guinea-Bissau's membership.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

Women's War of 1929 (Igbo Women's Uprising) Uprising · 1929

According to an article by Emily Manktelow published on the University of Kent School of History blog (2018-03-08), in late 1929 thousands of Igbo women rose up against a tax movement targeting women's economic activities (palm oil sales) and corruption among 'warrant chiefs' appointed under indirect rule introduced by Lugard in 1914, using a traditional ritual protest called 'sitting on men.' The British called it the 'Aba Women's Riot.' The women attacked native court buildings, cut telegraph lines, and destroyed banks, post offices, and factories. On December 16 in Oporoza, colonial troops killed 18 women, and British forces burned down the village as collective punishment. Subsequently, the British reformed the warrant chief system and abolished women's taxation.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other
Women's War FatalitiesColonial authorities' total unverified in original textOporoza, December 16: 18 (Manktelow 2018); overall total unverified in original text

Data Record: Because this was unarmed resistance during the colonial period, it is not recorded under any event unit in COW, UCDP, or NAVCO (which records campaigns from 1900 onward but does not include this event).

  1. Emily Manktelow, 'The Women's War, 1929', University of Kent School of History blog (2018-03-08) · Academic contribution · Orientation: Gender history and critical colonial perspective — https://blogs.kent.ac.uk/history/2018/03/08/the-womens-war-1929/

Two Coup Attempts in 1966 Coups · 1966

The Powell & Thyne coup data records two successful coups on January 15 and July 29, 1966. UCDP codes the government's conflict with a 'military faction' (the faction of Emmanuel Ifeajuna) in 1966 as the start of a government conflict. The casualty figures and scale of the Igbo massacres that followed in the north could not be verified from original sources in this round.

COW Civil War v5.1 records combat deaths in the '1967–1970 Biafran War' at 45,000. UCDP codes the territorial conflict between the government and the Republic of Biafra from 1967 onward, extending under the same conflict ID to IPOB (Igbo People's Organization) activities in the 2020s, coded as 1967–2025. Estimates of total deaths including famine and disease deaths vary widely across sources, and could not be verified from original texts in this round.

Boko Haram Uprising in July 2009 and the Death of Muhammad Yusuf Uprising · 2009

According to Al Jazeera (2009-07-31), after Boko Haram fighters launched organized attacks in four northern states, security forces attacked the group's base and mosque in Maiduguri, leaving hundreds dead in the clashes. Police announced that leader Mohammed Yusuf had died in a shootout while fleeing, dismissing claims of extrajudicial killing while in custody as 'propaganda aimed at undermining security agencies.' Meanwhile, Reuters and local journalists reported seeing him held without visible injuries in a military barracks in Maiduguri, and a BBC correspondent reported seeing footage of him being shot after confessing. Human Rights Watch characterized this as an 'extra-judicial execution' and called for an investigation. UCDP subsequently continued to record the conflict against JAS (Boko Haram) and IS, coding 9 years between 2015 and 2025 as war years with more than 1,000 battle deaths.

2020 #EndSARS Protests and Lekki Toll Gate Shootings Protest · 2020

According to an ICIR (2021-11-15) report, the Lagos State #EndSARS Judicial Panel of Inquiry found that on October 20, 2020, at the Lekki Toll Gate, Nigerian military forces fired live ammunition into unarmed protesters waving the national flag and singing the national anthem, causing deaths and injuries, and deemed this an unjustifiable use of excessive force. The committee stated that the military blocked access for ambulances, police also shot and beat protesters, and soldiers collected casings to cover up the incident. The committee's tally confirmed 9 deaths, estimated 4 deaths, and a list of 48 casualties (24 wounded). Federal Information Minister Lai Mohammed claimed there was no incident and that it was a 'massacre without bodies,' and the federal government has consistently denied the killings.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The Chain of Coups and Irregular Regime Changes, 1974–1999 Coups · 1974–1999

The Powell & Thyne coup data record coups in Niger on April 15, 1974 (successful), March 15, 1976 (unsuccessful), October 5, 1983 (unsuccessful), January 27, 1996 (successful), and April 9, 1999 (successful). Archigos also records leadership changes on April 17, 1974, January 27, 1996, and around April 11, 1999. Casualties and numbers of detainees for individual coups could not be verified from the original sources in this round.

  1. Powell & Thyne, Global Instances of Coups · Academic Dataset · Orientation: Neutral Event Coding — https://www.uky.edu/~clthyn2/coup_data/home.htm

February 18, 2010 Coup Removing President Tanja Coup · 2010

According to an article by Kenya Capital FM reporting AFP coverage (2010-02-19), on Thursday, February 18, soldiers ousted President Mamadou Tandja, and the military regime announced the next day that the Council for the Restoration of Democracy (CSRD) had dissolved the government and decided to suspend the Constitution of the Sixth Republic. The squadron commander Salou Djibo, who led a heavily armed force and played a key role in the coup, became chairman of the council. Medical sources reported that at least three soldiers were killed and at least ten wounded in the gunfight. Tandja was detained at a barracks outside the capital Niamey, while ministers were held elsewhere.

Presidential Guard Coup of July 26, 2023 Coup · 2023

According to reports by Al Jazeera (2023-07-28), on Wednesday, July 26, the Presidential Guard under General Abdourahamane Tchiani detained elected President Mohamed Bazoum at the presidential palace in Niamey. On July 28, Tchiani appeared on state television as chairman of the 'National Council for the Defense of the Homeland' and announced that he had become head of the transitional government, criticizing the government's security response as necessary to prevent the country's 'gradual and inevitable disappearance.' No timeline for a return to civilian rule was presented. Spokesman Captain Amadou Abdramane announced a suspension of the constitution, closure of borders, a nationwide curfew, and suspension of state institutions. The article reports that leaders inside and outside Africa issued statements opposing the detention of the president. The article does not report casualty figures.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The 1979–1980 rice riots and the coup by Colonel Doe Coup · 1979–1980

The Powell & Thyne coup data records the successful coup of April 12, 1980, while Archigos captures the irregular transfer of power on the same day. A year earlier, on April 14, 1979, a protest called by the Liberia Progressive Alliance against the government's rice subsidy price increase turned into a violent affair known as the 'rice riots.' However, because public sources detailing the circumstances and number of fatalities could not be accessed in this round, these remain unconfirmed. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) set its mandate period from 1979 to 2003.

Two Civil Wars in 1989–1996 and 1999–2003 Civil War · 1989–2003

The CRIN compilation of Truth and Reconciliation Commission data indicates that Liberia experienced two armed conflicts, in 1989–1996 and 1999–2003, and that the TRC investigated social unrest from 1979 to 2003. The same source cites Human Rights Watch to report that violence 'displaced nearly half of the population,' with tens of thousands of civilians suffering harm. This page does not present a total death toll.

Final Report of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2009) Civil War · 2008–2009

According to a press release from the Liberian Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2009-12-01), the commission submitted Volume I (preliminary report) to the government on December 20, 2008, and Volume II (integrated final report) on June 29, 2009; an unedited version was released on June 30, 2009. The report consists of approximately 1,500 pages across 21 chapters and contains 142 recommendations. It proposed indictments for 116 individuals before a special criminal court, 58 before domestic courts, public sanctions against 49 who supported armed factions, prosecution of 45 on economic crimes, and further investigation of 54. Of the approximately 103,019 combatants disarmed by UNMIL, about 7,000 were recommended for the community reconciliation program 'Palava Hut'.

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The 1968–2021 Coup Chain Coups · 1968–2021

The Powell & Thyne coup data records coups in Mali on November 19, 1968 (successful), February 15, 1978 (unsuccessful), March 26, 1991 (successful), July 14, 1991 (unsuccessful), March 22, 2012 (successful), May 1, 2012 (unsuccessful), August 18, 2020 (successful), and May 21, 2021 (successful). Archigos records the transitions from Modibo Kéita to Moussa Traoré in 1968, from Traoré to Alpha Oumar Konaré in 1991, and from Touré to Sanaogo in 2012 on the same dates. The coups of 1991, 2012, and 2020 each occurred immediately after large-scale protests or a northern armed uprising (see individual entries below).

The March 1991 Revolution — Bamako Protests and the Collapse of the Traoré Regime Regime Overthrow · 1991

According to the Swarthmore College Nonviolent Action Database, student union (AEEM) leaders were arrested in protests and unrest in late January 1991, and negotiations between the government and democratization groups broke down in late February. On March 17, a funeral march for 'Martyrs' Day' drew approximately 100,000 people. On March 22, soldiers fired on a march of tens of thousands, killing at least 22 (AP), and a curfew and state of emergency were declared. On March 23, five women were killed by soldiers in a peace march of about 2,000 women, and on March 24, soldiers set fire to a shop where protesters had taken refuge, killing dozens. A general strike by workers and a rally of approximately 45,000 followed on March 25, and on March 26, some soldiers sided with the protesters as a group of lieutenants led by Amadou Toumani Touré arrested Traoré. Following the legalization of opposition parties and the establishment of the National Assembly on a new constitution, Alpha Oumar Konaré of ADEMA was elected president in the April 1992 multiparty elections.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources

Northern Armed Uprising and the March 22 Coup of 2012 Civil War · 2012–2013

According to Human Rights Watch (2012-04-30), in January 2012, the Tuareg separatist group MNLA rose up demanding an independent state in the north, and Islamist groups demanding the application of sharia, Ansar Dine, and Arab militias around Timbuktu joined in. On March 22, junior officers staged a coup protesting the government's handling of the rebellion; Kidal (March 30), Gao (March 31), and Timbuktu (April 1) fell to rebels thereafter. According to OCHA estimates, at least 284,000 people had fled their homes since January, with approximately 107,000 internally displaced and approximately 177,000 seeking refuge in Niger, Burkina Faso, Algeria, and Mauritania. HRW documented the deaths of four patients at Gao hospital after staff left, two executions by Ansar Dine, and testimony that at least four Tuareg men were executed in Sévaré.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
Displaced Persons, Jan–Apr 2012Text not verified (Malian government announcement)At least 284,000 (approx. 107,000 internally displaced, approx. 177,000 externally displaced; OCHA estimates cited by HRW)
War Battle DeathsText not verifiedCOW 1,080 (2012–2013, data table)

Data Record: COW records the conflict as the 'North Mali War of 2012-2013' (internationalized, 1,080 battle deaths), while UCDP divides it into a territorial dispute (ID 372, 1990–2015) and a government insurgency (ID 11347, AQIM and Ansar Dine, 2009–2025). The same 2012 events are split into two conflict streams in UCDP.

2020 M5-RFP Protests and the August 18 Coup Protest · 2020

According to Human Rights Watch (2020-08-12), the 'Movement of June 5 for Patriotic Forces Rallying' (M5-RFP), an alliance of opposition parties, religious leaders, and civil society groups, led protests from June 2020 onward, sometimes demanding the resignation of President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta; Imam Mahmoud Dicko is cited as a leader. On July 10–12 in Bamako, protesters erected barricades and burned parts of government buildings while security forces used tear gas and live ammunition. President Keïta promised an investigation on July 11, and the Prime Minister's office announced an investigation into allegations of deployment of the anti-terror special forces (FORSAT) on July 14. M5-RFP leaders stated that participants in street violence were not affiliated with their movement. The Keïta government fell in an August 18 coup (P&T record).

5. Modern Events through the Literature

The 1978–2008 Coup Chain Coups · 1978–2008

The Powell & Thyne coup data record coups in Mauritania on July 10, 1978 (successful), January 4, 1980 (successful), February 6, 1982 (failed), December 12, 1984 (successful), June 8, 2003 (failed), August 3, 2005 (successful), and August 6, 2008 (successful). Archigos records the exit of the first president, Moktar Ould Daddah, on July 10, 1978; internal changes within the military committee in April and June 1979; the accession of Moktar Ould Haidalla on January 4, 1980; and the accession of Mohamed Ould Abdel Aziz (Taya) on December 12, 1984, as part of the same trajectory. The 1978 coup occurred during the Western Sahara War (UCDP's POLISARIO conflict). Casualty figures for individual coups could not be verified from the original sources in this round.

The 1989–1991 Expulsion of Black Mauritanians and Mass Detention and Executions within the Military ('Passif humanitaire') Uprising · 1989–1993

According to the Middle East and North Africa human rights group MENA Rights Group, at the end of the 1980s the government expelled more than 60,000 Mauritanians from the Halpulaar, Soninke, and Wolof communities. From October 1990 through mid-January 1991, authorities arrested approximately 3,000 Black African soldiers on suspicion of plotting a coup; an estimated 500–600 were summarily executed, and the survivors were released under a presidential amnesty in March–April 1991. On November 28, 1990 (Inal), 28 Black African soldiers were summarily executed at a military base. Law No. 93-23 of June 14, 1993 pardoned crimes committed by security forces during this period. The Mauritanian authorities maintain that they have provided justice and appropriate reparations to the victims (letter to UN Special Rapporteur on September 23, 2020), but victim organizations counter that reparations cannot substitute for effective redress. Accounts diverge between the government narrative (a response to coup plotting) and the victim narrative (racial repression), and this Country Analysis Series makes no determination.

Expulsions in the late 1980sOriginal text unconfirmedMore than 60,000 (MENA Rights Group)

5. Modern Events as Seen in the Literature

The 1963–1975 Coup Chain and the 2025 Coup Attempt Coups · 1963–2025

The Powell & Thyne coup data record successful coups on October 28, 1963, November 29, 1965, December 22, 1965, December 17, 1967, December 10, 1969, and October 26, 1972, in Dahomey (now Benin), as well as failed coups on February 23, 1972, and January 21, 1975, and a failed coup on December 7, 2025. Archigos records frequent leadership changes: Maga to Soglo in 1963, through Apithy and Congoou to Soglo in 1965, Allè in 1967, and Zinsou in 1968. The Mathieu Kérékou regime, which took power in the October 1972 coup, continued into the 1989–1990 democratization movement below. Casualty figures for the 1960s coups could not be verified from the original sources in this round.

ItemOfficial AnnouncementsIndependent Investigations & Other Sources
